cURL HTTP curl https://api.tapeapp.com/v1/record/1 \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TAPE_TOKEN" GET /v1/record/1 HTTP/1.1 Host: api.tapeapp.com Authorization: Bearer tape_pat_0a1b2c3d... $TAPE_TOKEN holds your personal access token from the Quickstart. 1 is a record ID. An OAuth access token goes in the same header. So does a user API key in existing integrations: curl https://api.tapeapp.com/v1/record/1 \ -H "Authorization: Bearer tape_oat_0a1b2c3d..."

You are… Use A developer calling the API directly: a script, an internal tool, an integration you build and run, including one that works in Tape on a user's behalf A personal access token Connecting an AI assistant or another MCP client to Tape OAuth: the client signs in with Tape Building an integration or partner product that Tape registers, with a "Connect to Tape" or "Sign in with Tape" button OAuth, with a client registered by Tape Maintaining an integration built on a user API key Keep it running, and move it to a personal access token when you next work on it Personal access tokens are the default. Use one whenever you write code that calls the Tape API. A personal access token: needs no client registration, no redirect and no consent screen never needs refreshing can be limited to the capabilities, workspaces and apps your code needs can be revoked on its own without affecting anything else The user your integration should act as creates the token and hands it to your integration. Coming from the Podio API? Instead of app authentication, use a personal access token limited to that app. OAuth is for MCP clients and registered integrations. With OAuth, a person connects an app by signing in to Tape, without handling a secret. MCP clients use it to connect to the Tape MCP server. Integrations and partners registered by Tape use it for their sign-in. Building such an integration? Ask Tape to register a client.

Personal access token OAuth access token User API key Used by Developers calling the API directly MCP clients, and integrations registered by Tape Existing integrations Prefix tape_pat_ tape_oat_ user_key_ Obtained by Creating it in your Tape settings The user approving your app on Tape's consent screen Copying it from your Tape settings What it may do Only the capabilities you grant it Only the capabilities the user approved Everything your user account can do What it may reach All, or only the workspaces and apps you select Everything the user can reach Everything you can reach Lifetime Until revoked Access tokens last one hour and are renewed with a refresh token; the connection ends after 90 days unused, and for most apps a year after approval Until deleted Revoking Individually, at any time By the user, an organization admin, or the app Only by deleting the single key Status Recommended For MCP clients and registered integrations Deprecated, existing integrations only User API keys are deprecated Existing user API keys keep working, but you can't limit them to capabilities, workspaces or apps. Deleting a key breaks every integration that uses it. Build new integrations on a personal access token.

Each Tape user has one user API key. It acts as a bearer token for the API. Where do you find the user API key? Select your profile picture, then select Preferences. In the settings window, select Developer (under Features). If you still have a user API key, it appears as API Key in the table of personal access tokens. Open its ⋯ menu and select Copy API key or Delete. Keep your user API key secret Your user API key has the same privileges as your user account. If it leaks, delete it in the settings window under Developer and create a personal access token instead. A deleted key can't be restored.

A personal access token is a named credential you create for one integration. You choose what it may do, and which workspaces and apps it may reach. Tokens start with tape_pat_, and Tape shows each one only once, when you create it. Personal access tokens: create, limit and revoke a token. Capabilities: the full list of what you can grant a token.

An app receives an OAuth access token when a Tape user connects it to their account: The app sends the user to Tape. The user approves the scopes the app asked for. The app gets an access token that acts as that user. Tokens start with tape_oat_, last one hour, and are renewed with a refresh token. OAuth describes the whole flow.

An automation API key authenticates an automation, not a person. Tape creates a new one for each automation run. Keys start with workflow_key_ and expire after a short time. The tape client in an Execute a script action uses it, so your script doesn't handle authentication. You can't create, copy or revoke an automation API key yourself. The key has no user behind it, so endpoints that need a user reject it, mostly with 400 or 401. Where it works, Tape checks the automation's own access to the app or record. It works for: the discovery endpoints of the automation API calling an automation and generating a weblink listing the views of an app retrieving a single app the record endpoints the built-in actions call: retrieve, create, update, delete and restore a record, filter records, retrieve the records of a view, record references and their statistics batch creating and batch updating records all record revision endpoints unfollowing all records in a database app creating a comment or a reply, and deleting a comment or reply generating a PDF, sending an email and making an authenticated HTTP call uploading files and creating a signed upload URL the automation usage report It doesn't work for managing apps, fields and views, retrieving a view, retrieving shared records, finding relatable records, updating record permissions, reading or listing comments and replies, deleting a comment with DELETE /v1/comment/{comment_id}, managing automations, listing automation runs, search, webhooks, users, workspaces and organizations. Requests with an automation API key count against the run's own budget, not a user's. The X-RateLimit-Scope header shows workflow. See Request limits.

Every credential belongs to a user. Changes made with it show that user as the author, for example in the record's activity. You also don't get notifications for your own changes on records you follow. To show an integration under its own name, create a dedicated user, for example "API User", and create the credential from that account.

Failed authentication with a personal access token or a user API key returns one of these responses. An OAuth access token that's no longer valid gets its own response. See General behavior. Invalid or unusable credential { "status_code": 400, "endpoint": "/v1/record/1", "error_code": "validation", "error_message": "Invalid API key for accessing endpoint '/v1/record/1' (no active user for the given API key)" } Malformed credential { "status_code": 400, "endpoint": "/v1/record/1", "error_code": "validation", "error_message": "Invalid API key for accessing endpoint '/v1/record/1' (signature check not passed, key is malformed)" } Missing credential { "status_code": 401, "endpoint": "/v1/record/1", "error_code": "dev_api_authentication", "error_message": "Missing authentication for Dev-API endpoint: '/v1/record/1' (no user API key provided)" } The missing authentication response also carries WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="https://api.tapeapp.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/v1". An OAuth client finds Tape's authorization server there. Why do several causes return the same message? An unknown token, a revoked token and a token whose owner was deactivated all return the same "no active user for the given API key" message. This is deliberate: different messages would let an unauthenticated caller probe which tokens exist. Getting an error? Authentication error Check that you send the whole token, prefix included, after Bearer . If the token was revoked or lost, create a new one under Developer.

An OAuth access token that's no longer valid (expired, revoked or disconnected) returns 401 with the error code dev_api_invalid_access_token. The response carries a WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token" header, whose resource_metadata points to the Developer API's protected resource metadata. See Errors at the Developer API. A personal access token or OAuth access token that authenticates but lacks the capability an endpoint requires returns 403. See Insufficient capabilities.

Quickstart make your first request with a personal access token. Personal access tokens create and limit a token. Capabilities what each endpoint requires. OAuth overview connect apps and MCP clients. Errors handle all error codes.

A credential acts as the user it belongs to. Its effective access is that user's own permissions, narrowed by its capabilities: Axis Question it answers Personal access token OAuth access token The user's own role What may this person do anyway? Applies Applies Capabilities What kind of action? Chosen at creation Approved at consent Content access Which workspaces and apps? All, or only the ones you select Everything the user can reach A capability never gives a credential access to something its user can't reach. When the user loses access to a workspace, every credential they own loses it too.

Area Capability Scope What it allows Organization Read organization organization:read View your organization and its members, including their names, email addresses and phone numbers. Manage members organization.members:manage Invite people to your organization and manage invitations. Invitations can take up paid seats. Workspaces Read workspaces workspaces:read View workspaces and their members. Edit workspaces workspaces:edit Create, rename and delete workspaces. Deleting a workspace also deletes the apps and records inside it. Manage members workspaces.members:manage Add and remove workspace members. This gives other people access. Apps Read apps apps:read View apps together with their fields, views and settings. Also search across them. Edit apps apps:edit Create, edit and delete apps, fields and views. Deleting a field also deletes its values in every record, and they cannot be restored. Records Read records records:read View records, their field values, files and full revision history, including values that were deleted. Also search across them. Edit records records:edit Create, edit, delete and restore records, and upload files. Read comments records.comments:read View comments and replies on records. Edit comments records.comments:edit Post comments and replies, and delete your own. Share records records:share Change who can see and edit individual records. This gives other people access. Automations Read automations automations:read View automations, their run history and their setup, including credentials for connected systems. Edit automations automations:edit Create, edit, activate, deactivate and delete automations. Deactivating one stops the processes that depend on it. Run automations automations:run Trigger and simulate automations on your behalf. An automation runs with the rights of the person who owns it, so it can do things the credential cannot, including in apps outside a token's content access. Advanced Manage webhooks webhooks:manage Create, list, verify and delete webhooks. A webhook keeps sending record, comment and app changes to an address you choose until someone deletes it, including after the credential that created it is revoked. Send email email:send Send email on your behalf, using your organization's email settings. Without your own SMTP server, Tape sends from its own address.

Editing doesn't include reading. records:edit lets a credential write records, but not read them back. A write-only integration, such as an inbound sync, needs no read access. Grant both when you need both. Deleting is part of editing. There's no separate delete capability. records:edit covers creating, changing, deleting and restoring records. workspaces:edit covers deleting a workspace and everything inside it. Identifying yourself needs nothing. GET /v1/user tells you which user a credential belongs to and requires no capability. It returns no other user. Search is filtered, not blocked. /v1/search returns app and record results. It accepts a credential that holds either apps:read or records:read, and returns only the result types the credential may see. A credential with only records:read gets record results and no app results.

A personal access token gets its capabilities from the checkboxes in the settings. An OAuth app requests them in the scope parameter of its authorization request: scope=apps:read records:read records:edit

Separate scopes with a single space (%20 in a URL). Tabs, line breaks and other whitespace make the value unknown. Use the scope strings from the table above. Omitting scope grants the read tier, apps:read records:read. So does a scope that's empty once Tape removes ignored values. Tape ignores OpenID Connect values. It drops openid, profile, email, address, phone and offline_access without an error, because many client libraries send them unasked. Tape isn't an OpenID provider, and it issues a refresh token without offline_access. Any other unknown value fails the request with invalid_scope. The user approves all requested scopes or none. The consent screen lists the requested scopes one per line, so sending email, managing webhooks and inviting organization members each get their own line. An MCP client that requests exactly the scopes the Tape MCP server advertises sees a short fixed summary instead. Read scope in the token response instead of assuming Tape granted your request as sent. It names exactly what the access token holds. Request every scope your app needs in the first authorization. Scopes are fixed once the user approves. To add one later, the user has to approve again; see Insufficient capabilities.

A credential that authenticates but lacks a capability the endpoint requires gets a 403. The message names the kind of credential: Response { "status_code": 403, "endpoint": "/v1/record/1", "error_code": "forbidden", "error_message": "This personal access token is missing the required scope(s): records:edit." } For an OAuth access token, the message reads This OAuth access token is missing the required scope(s): records:edit. Some endpoints accept any one of several capabilities, such as /v1/search. They refuse a credential that holds none of them with a message that lists them all. The response also carries a standard WWW-Authenticate header that names what the endpoint needs: WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="insufficient_scope", error_description="This personal access token is missing the required scope(s): records:edit.", scope="records:edit" The scope value lists what the endpoint requires, not what your credential holds. Among 403 responses, only a capability refusal carries this header. See 403 and 404 mean different things. A refused request still costs credits Tape checks capabilities after rate limiting, so a 403 uses rate limit credits like any other request. Retrying a call your credential can't make uses up your budget without ever succeeding.

Personal access token. A token's capabilities are fixed when you create it. You can only change its name afterwards. Create a new token with the capabilities your integration needs, switch to it, and revoke the old one. OAuth access token. Send the user through a new authorization request whose scope names the scopes the app already holds plus the missing one (step-up authorization). Approval creates a new connection with exactly those scopes. Revoke the earlier connection's refresh token once you've stored the new tokens; see Asking for more scopes. The Tape MCP server answers a missing scope with a 403 whose scope already names the full set.

A request passes through independent checks. The status code and the WWW-Authenticate header together tell you which check refused it: Status Meaning Fix 403 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="insufficient_scope" and a scope value The credential lacks a capability the endpoint requires Create a token with that capability, or ask the user to approve it 403 without that header The user's own role or permissions in Tape do not allow this operation, for example changing a view needs share access (Can share or Full access) to its app. error_message says why Change the user's access in Tape. A new token or a new approval doesn't help 404 The resource does not exist, the user cannot see it, or, for a personal access token, it is outside the token's content access Check the user's access; for a token, create one that selects that workspace or app A 404 deliberately looks the same as a resource that doesn't exist, so it carries no WWW-Authenticate header. If a personal access token gets a 404 for a record or app you know exists, check the token's content access first. An OAuth access token has no content access, so a 404 is about the user's own access. A missing permission on a record or app usually returns 400 with record_no_permission or app_no_permission, not 403. See Errors.

A few internal endpoints refuse personal access tokens and OAuth access tokens, whatever capabilities they hold. They're not part of the public API. Requests to them return a 403 with this message: This endpoint cannot be accessed with a personal access token. For an OAuth access token, the message is This endpoint cannot be accessed with an OAuth access token. Every endpoint in this reference is reachable with the right capability.

Personal access tokens create a token with the capabilities you need. Authorization flow request scopes for your app. Authentication compare the three credentials. Errors handle 403, 404 and other errors. Request limits what refused requests cost.

Format Shape Example Used for Datetime YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm:ss 2021-03-04 05:30:00 A point in time. Date YYYY-MM-DD 2021-03-04 The date part of a value; a calendar day. Time HH:mm:ss 05:30:00 The time-of-day part of a value. The datetime format is close to ISO 8601, but not identical: 2021-03-04 05:30:00 ← Tape 2021-03-04T05:30:00Z ← the equivalent in standardized ISO 8601 A space replaces the T separator. There's no Z suffix, no numeric offset, and no fractional seconds, so the property name, not the string, tells you the zone. Do responses include seconds? Datetime properties in responses include :ss, also when it's 00: 2021-03-04 05:30:00, never 2021-03-04 05:30. Seconds are optional in request bodies, but don't expect the shorter form back. The exception is the pre-formatted value / value_string of a calculation field value. It's a display string without seconds (YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm, or YYYY-MM-DD for a whole day).

The API returns every temporal property twice, with the same rule everywhere: The unsuffixed property (start, created_on, due_at, logged_at) is the value in the acting user's timezone. Use it for display. The _utc property (start_utc, created_on_utc, due_at_utc, logged_at_utc) is the same instant in UTC. Use it to compare, sort, store and calculate. Only two places break this rule. Field values give each half at three levels of detail: the full datetime, the date part and the time part. A date field value carries six properties per date: Property Timezone Format Example start acting user YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm:ss 2021-03-03 22:30:00 start_date acting user YYYY-MM-DD 2021-03-03 start_time acting user HH:mm:ss 22:30:00 start_utc UTC YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm:ss 2021-03-04 05:30:00 start_date_utc UTC YYYY-MM-DD 2021-03-04 start_time_utc UTC HH:mm:ss 05:30:00 A range_date field value repeats all six with an end prefix: end, end_date, end_time, end_utc, end_date_utc, end_time_utc. Single-instant properties elsewhere in the API come as a pair: created_on / created_on_utc, completed_at / completed_at_utc, and so on. The two halves can disagree on the calendar day The example above is one instant, 2021-03-04 05:30:00 UTC, read by a user in America/Phoenix (UTC-7). The local half falls on March 3rd, the UTC half on March 4th. Grouping by start_date and by start_date_utc gives different groups. Which values should an integration read? Read _utc and convert to your own display timezone. The unsuffixed values depend on whose credential is in use, so they're a poor fit for anything cached, compared or stored. Daylight saving shows why: the local half of a stored instant shifts by an hour twice a year, while its _utc half never moves.
documents.s: Local and UTC are returned side by side

documents.t: The timezone comes from the timezone setting of the user who owns the credential. It's not part of the request: There's no header, query parameter or body property that sets the timezone on /v1/* routes. Two credentials of two users with different timezone settings return different unsuffixed values for the same record. The _utc values are identical. For an automation API key, Tape uses the automation's timezone. No endpoint reports the timezone. To find the offset your credential uses, compare the two halves of any timestamp, for example created_on and created_on_utc on any record.

One record, read with two credentials: one owned by a user set to America/Phoenix, one by a user set to Europe/Amsterdam. Phoenix (UTC-7) { "record_id": 1, "created_on": "2021-03-03 22:30:00", "created_on_utc": "2021-03-04 05:30:00", "fields": [ { "field_id": 2, "external_id": "event_date", "type": "date", "field_type": "single_date", "values": [ { "start": "2021-03-03 22:30:00", "start_date": "2021-03-03", "start_time": "22:30:00", "start_utc": "2021-03-04 05:30:00", "start_date_utc": "2021-03-04", "start_time_utc": "05:30:00" } ] } ] } Amsterdam (UTC+1) { "record_id": 1, "created_on": "2021-03-04 06:30:00", "created_on_utc": "2021-03-04 05:30:00", "fields": [ { "field_id": 2, "external_id": "event_date", "type": "date", "field_type": "single_date", "values": [ { "start": "2021-03-04 06:30:00", "start_date": "2021-03-04", "start_time": "06:30:00", "start_utc": "2021-03-04 05:30:00", "start_date_utc": "2021-03-04", "start_time_utc": "05:30:00" } ] } ] }

Two places don't return a local and a UTC value side by side. Both are deliberate. Where Behavior Calculation field value: value, value_string Pre-formatted display strings, built from the local start_date / start_time and rendered without seconds. They have no _utc sibling. To compare or store a calculation date result, read start_utc from the same value object rather than parsing value. Automation usage report: from, to Edges of the reporting intervals that had activity in the bucket, not event timestamps and not the edges of the calendar bucket. The _utc siblings exist so the API is uniform, but all four values are UTC.

Property names use two suffixes for the same concept: created_on in some places, created_at in others. The split is historical, not meaningful. _on: the earliest resources, such as records, comments, replies, revisions, files, organizations, and attachment and image previews. _at: resources and values added later, such as automations and runs, checklist entries, calculation script config, and the authorship metadata on email, phone and link values. Both use the same formats and meaning, and both have a _utc sibling.

A date field value holds either a point in time or a whole calendar day without a time. The API has no all_day flag. Two signals mark a calendar day: start_time and start_time_utc are null. The local and UTC halves are identical. Tape doesn't convert a calendar day between timezones: March 4th is March 4th for every user, in every zone. A whole day — 2021-03-04 { "start": "2021-03-04 00:00:00", "start_date": "2021-03-04", "start_time": null, "start_utc": "2021-03-04 00:00:00", "start_date_utc": "2021-03-04", "start_time_utc": null } A point in time — 2021-03-04 at midnight UTC, read in Amsterdam { "start": "2021-03-04 01:00:00", "start_date": "2021-03-04", "start_time": "01:00:00", "start_utc": "2021-03-04 00:00:00", "start_date_utc": "2021-03-04", "start_time_utc": "00:00:00" } start is a midnight timestamp even for a whole day A calendar day still returns start and start_utc as a full YYYY-MM-DD 00:00:00 datetime. From start alone, you can't tell a whole day from a real midnight timestamp, as the second example shows. Test start_time === null, or read the date-only start_date. A range_date value of whole days follows the same rule on both ends: start_time and end_time are both null, and every local property equals its _utc twin. A range can't mix a whole-day start with a timed end. Both ends are the same kind. Checklist entry due dates use the same convention on due_at_time / due_at_time_utc.

Requests accept the same three formats: Input Interpreted as "2021-03-04" A whole calendar day. "2021-03-04 05:30" A point in time. Seconds may be omitted. "2021-03-04 05:30:00" A point in time. "2021-03-04 - 2021-03-06" A range. Split on a hyphen surrounded by single spaces. Field values you write are read as UTC, not as your timezone By default, Tape stores a datetime you send as UTC. Send "2021-03-04 05:30:00" as a user in Europe/Amsterdam, and the record reads back as 06:30:00 in start and 05:30:00 in start_utc. Date filters, by contrast, are read in your timezone. Convert to UTC before sending, or add the query parameter apply_user_timezone_on_date_inputs=true to the record create and update endpoints (single and batch). Tape then reads a datetime without an offset in the calling user's timezone. The parameter applies to date, date range and checklist due date values. start_utc, end_utc and due_at_utc properties, and values that state their own offset, aren't shifted. The field's time setting also decides whether a written value becomes a calendar day or a timestamp. See Date field. settings.time Effect on a written value disabled Stored as a calendar day. Tape discards any time component you send. enabled A bare YYYY-MM-DD is stored as a calendar day; anything with a time as a timestamp. required Stored as a timestamp. A bare YYYY-MM-DD becomes midnight UTC. Field values also accept an object form. A _utc property in it takes precedence over its unsuffixed counterpart, so you can write a value read from the API straight back unchanged. See Date field value for the accepted object shapes.

Endpoints that accept a date window take each bound in both forms. Search accepts all eight parameters below. The general automation run listing accepts the four created_at_* bounds only. Parameter Read as created_at_from Your timezone created_at_from_utc UTC created_at_to Your timezone created_at_to_utc UTC last_modified_at_from Your timezone last_modified_at_from_utc UTC last_modified_at_to Your timezone last_modified_at_to_utc UTC

All bounds use YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm:ss and are inclusive. Each bound is independent. Send only a _from for "since", only a _to for "until", or both for a closed window. A _from later than its matching _to returns 400. Tape reads the unsuffixed form in the same timezone it uses for created_on. A value taken from a result means the same instant when you send it back as a bound. If you send both forms of the same bound, the _utc one wins. Polling for changes? Use the _utc bounds: a wall-clock time carries no offset, so it's ambiguous when daylight saving ends and the same local hour occurs twice. Pass last_modified_at_from_utc with the last_modified_on_utc of your last result. The loop then never reads a window twice or skips one.
Automations use the same paired local and UTC variables. Scripts run in UTC, so convert a local time before you write it. See Date, time & timezones.

Date field value the accepted object shapes for dates. Date field the time setting of a date field. Search filter by creation and change dates. Record create and update records with dates. Date, time & timezones dates in automations.

Status error_code Description 400 validation The request is not valid: the body is not valid JSON, doesn't match the expected parameters, or the credential is invalid, malformed or can't be used for this endpoint. Check the error_message property for details. 400 input_validation The body doesn't match the endpoint's schema. error_message starts with Invalid input: and names each property that fails, for example data/name must NOT have fewer than 1 characters. 400 bad_request The request is malformed, for example an empty records array in a batch request. 400 record_no_permission / app_no_permission The user has no permission for this record or app. 400 record_deleted The record is in the trash. 400 workspace_invalid_permission The user has no permission for this workspace, for example no Admin role in it. 400 deletions_rejected The request was sent with reject_deletions=true and would delete a field or an option. Tape applies nothing from the request. See Update an app. 401 dev_api_authentication The request carries no personal access token, OAuth access token or user API key. 401 unauthorized The credential type isn't accepted for this endpoint (for example an automation API key on an endpoint that needs a credential acting for a user), or the user may not perform this operation. error_message says why. 401 dev_api_invalid_access_token The OAuth access token is expired, revoked or otherwise no longer valid. Refresh it, or connect again. See OAuth errors. 403 forbidden The request is not allowed. If the response carries WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="insufficient_scope", the personal access token or OAuth access token lacks a capability this endpoint requires. See Insufficient capabilities. Otherwise the operation was refused for another reason, such as the user's permissions; error_message says why. 404 not_found The resource doesn't exist, isn't shared with the owner of the credential, or lies outside a personal access token's content access. An unknown path, or a method a path doesn't support, also returns not_found (for example Cannot GET /v1/recrods). 404 record_not_exists The requested record doesn't exist. 404 app_not_exists The requested app doesn't exist. 409 conflict The resource is in a state that doesn't allow this operation, for example activating or running a broken automation. 429 user_too_many_requests This request exceeds the number of requests allowed. Wait the seconds in the Retry-After header, then retry. See rate limits. 500 unknown An unexpected error occurred. Reach out to Tape support.

Endpoints can return other, more specific error_code values. Handle an unknown error_code by its HTTP status. A missing permission on a record or app returns 400, not 403. Check error_code to tell it apart from other 400 errors. A request body that isn't valid JSON returns 400 with validation. The message starts with "A valid JSON body is required for operation". Getting an error? 403 error Check the WWW-Authenticate header. With insufficient_scope, fix the missing capability: create a new token, or ask the user of an OAuth app to approve it. Without that header, the user's own permissions in Tape refuse the request.
Capabilities the capability each endpoint requires. Authentication send a valid credential. Request limits avoid 429 responses. Authorization flow refresh an expired access token.

Send every request to the base URL https://api.tapeapp.com. The API requires HTTPS. The API follows RESTful conventions where possible. Most operations use GET, POST, PUT and DELETE requests. Request and response bodies are JSON.

Property names use snake_case, not camelCase or kebab-case. Dates and datetimes are strings in an ISO 8601-like format. A datetime includes the time (2020-08-12 02:12:33), a date only the date (2020-08-12). See Date & timezone.

Every endpoint shows a sample request and response. Requests use cURL. The samples use a personal access token, the recommended credential. Send it as a bearer token in the Authorization header, or with the cURL option -u (-u tape_pat_…:). A user API key works the same way. Most samples read the token from the environment variable TAPE_TOKEN and use example IDs such as 1. Replace them with your own.

Quickstart: retrieve your first record. Coming from the Podio API: move an existing integration to Tape. Tape API guide, first steps: try three requests in Postman, no code needed. Authentication: choose between personal access tokens, user API keys and OAuth. Capabilities: what each endpoint requires. Errors: status codes and error codes. Request limits: stay within the request budget. Pagination: page through long lists. In the Help Center: Tape API In the Help Center: Intro to Tape for developers

Create a fresh random code verifier for every authorization. Derive its code challenge from it: BASE64URL(SHA256(code_verifier)), without padding. Keep the verifier on your side until the code exchange, in your backend session or in the app's memory. code_verifier=$(openssl rand -base64 48 | tr '+/' '-_' | tr -d '=\n') code_challenge=$(printf '%s' "$code_verifier" | openssl dgst -sha256 -binary | openssl base64 | tr '+/' '-_' | tr -d '=\n') The verifier must be 43 to 128 characters from A–Z, a–z, 0–9 and -._~. The challenge has 43 characters.
documents.s: Step 1: Create a code verifier and challenge

documents.t: Redirect the user's browser to the authorization endpoint: https://api.tapeapp.com/oauth/authorize ?response_type=code &client_id=tape_oc_8f14e45fceea167a5a36dedd4bea2543 &redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fapp.example.com%2Foauth%2Fcallback &scope=apps%3Aread%20records%3Aread%20records%3Aedit &state=af0ifjsldkj &code_challenge=E9Melhoa2OwvFrEMTJguCHaoeK1t8URWbuGJSstw-cM &code_challenge_method=S256 Parameter Required Description response_type Yes code. client_id Yes Your client ID. redirect_uri Yes One of your registered redirect URIs. Required even if you registered only one. code_challenge Yes The challenge from step 1. code_challenge_method Recommended S256. If omitted, Tape assumes S256. Tape refuses plain. state Recommended An unguessable value bound to the user's browser session. Tape returns it unchanged. Check it on the way back to prevent CSRF. scope No Space-separated scopes. Defaults to apps:read records:read. resource No https://api.tapeapp.com/v1 or https://mcp.tapeapp.com/mcp, and may repeat. Accepted for compatibility. The token works at both either way. Tape ignores other parameters, such as nonce.
documents.s: Step 2: Send the user to Tape

documents.t: Tape asks the user to sign in if needed. The Connect with Tape consent screen then shows the organization to connect under Select organization, and: Your app's name. For a self-registered client, it shows the client ID URL or the redirect host instead. A client Tape can't tie to a website carries the badge Unverified: one with a custom URL scheme shows that scheme, one that returns to a loopback address shows its software_id or the client_name it registered with, in lowercase. For a self-registered client, the screen reads Connect with Tape MCP. What your app can do, one line per scope you requested. The user approves all the requested scopes with Continue, or declines with Cancel. An authorization request expires if the user doesn't decide in time. Why can't some users approve? Organization guests can't connect apps. An organization can restrict apps. Owners and admins can allow only approved apps for new connections, or limit an app to owners and admins. The consent screen tells a blocked member why, and the member can ask an admin.

Tape redirects the browser to your redirect_uri: https://app.example.com/oauth/callback ?code=tape_oac_4b227777d4dd1fc61c6f884f48641d02b4d121d3fd328cb08b5531fcacdabf8a &state=af0ifjsldkj &iss=https%3A%2F%2Fapi.tapeapp.com Before you use the code, check two values: state is the value you sent. iss is https://api.tapeapp.com. If the user declines, you receive access_denied: https://app.example.com/oauth/callback ?error=access_denied &state=af0ifjsldkj &iss=https%3A%2F%2Fapi.tapeapp.com

An invalid request still reaches your app, for example an unknown scope, a malformed PKCE challenge, or an unsupported resource. Tape asks the user to sign in, then shows an error page with the reason ID. When the user selects Return to app, your redirect_uri receives error (invalid_request, invalid_scope, invalid_target or unsupported_response_type) and an error_description that ends in the reason ID. An untrusted client gets no redirect. When Tape can't trust the client_id or redirect_uri itself, because it is unknown, revoked, or not registered, the user sees an error page instead. A request that prefers application/json gets a 400 with an invalid_client body.

Post the code to the token endpoint within 60 seconds: Confidential client curl https://api.tapeapp.com/oauth/token \ -u "tape_oc_8f14e45fceea167a5a36dedd4bea2543:tape_ocs_..." \ -d grant_type=authorization_code \ -d code=tape_oac_4b2277... \ -d code_verifier="$code_verifier" \ -d redirect_uri=https://app.example.com/oauth/callback Public client curl https://api.tapeapp.com/oauth/token \ -d client_id=tape_oc_8f14e45fceea167a5a36dedd4bea2543 \ -d grant_type=authorization_code \ -d code=tape_oac_4b2277... \ -d code_verifier="$code_verifier" \ -d redirect_uri=https://app.example.com/oauth/callback redirect_uri is optional here. If you send it, it must equal the value from step 2 exactly. Response { "access_token": "tape_oat_9a3f...", "token_type": "Bearer", "expires_in": 3600, "refresh_token": "tape_ort_3f9a...", "scope": "apps:read records:read records:edit", "tape_user_id": 45, "tape_organization_id": 7 } Key fields Field Meaning access_token Send it as Authorization: Bearer to the API. expires_in Seconds until the access token expires, at most 3600. refresh_token Gets new access tokens. Store it securely, on your server where you can. scope The scopes this access token holds. Read it instead of assuming Tape granted your request as sent. tape_user_id The connected Tape user. Key your accounts on it: a person who belongs to two Tape organizations is two Tape users. tape_organization_id The organization the user chose on the consent screen. Never retry a code exchange A code is single use: Tape treats a code presented twice as stolen, even your own retry after a timeout. It then disconnects the connection the code created and answers invalid_grant. If an exchange fails, start a new authorization instead.
documents.s: Step 5: Exchange the code for tokens

documents.t: curl https://api.tapeapp.com/v1/user \ -H "Authorization: Bearer tape_oat_9a3f..." The token acts as the connected user, limited to the approved scopes. It works at the Developer API and the Tape MCP server alike. GET /v1/user needs no scope and reports the token's scopes in its response.

An access token lasts one hour. Get a new one with the refresh token: curl https://api.tapeapp.com/oauth/token \ -u "tape_oc_8f14e45fceea167a5a36dedd4bea2543:tape_ocs_..." \ -d grant_type=refresh_token \ -d refresh_token=tape_ort_3f9a... A public client sends -d client_id=tape_oc_... instead of -u, here and when disconnecting. What happens to the refresh token depends on your client type: Public clients rotate. Every refresh returns a new refresh token and uses up the one you sent, so store the new one every time. Re-sending a used refresh token within 30 seconds, for example as a retry after a timeout, returns a fresh pair, up to three times. Tape treats a later re-send, or a fourth one, as theft: it disconnects the connection for every device that holds it, and the user has to connect again. Confidential clients keep theirs. The refresh token from the code exchange stays valid for the life of the connection. A refresh returns only a new access token, without refresh_token. Concurrent refreshes are fine. Send scope to get an access token with fewer scopes than the connection holds. scope never adds scopes. A scope outside the connection fails with invalid_scope and leaves the refresh token usable.

Every refresh keeps the connection alive. A connection that gets no new token for 90 days expires. A connection also ends 365 days after the user approved it, however active it is. This doesn't apply when Tape registered your client as a confidential one. When a refresh fails with invalid_grant, the connection is gone. Send the user through the authorization flow again.

When your app calls an endpoint that needs a scope the token lacks, the API answers 403 with: WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="insufficient_scope", error_description="This OAuth access token is missing the required scope(s): records:edit.", scope="records:edit" To get the missing scope: Send the user through the authorization flow again. Set scope to the scopes you already hold plus the missing one. If you ask for the missing scope alone, you end up with only that scope. The user approves the new set. You get a new connection with exactly those scopes. Store the new tokens, then revoke the old refresh token. The new approval doesn't end the earlier connection, so the user would otherwise keep an unused one. Ask for everything you need up front, so you don't send the user back to the consent screen. See Insufficient capabilities.

To disconnect, revoke the refresh token: curl https://api.tapeapp.com/oauth/revoke \ -u "tape_oc_8f14e45fceea167a5a36dedd4bea2543:tape_ocs_..." \ -d token=tape_ort_3f9a... \ -d token_type_hint=refresh_token A refresh token ends the whole connection. Every access token issued for it stops working on the next request. An access token revokes only that one access token. The connection keeps working. Once your client authenticates and sends a token, the endpoint answers 200 with an empty body. This includes a token that is unknown, already revoked, or not your client's. A connection also ends when: the user disconnects your app in Tape, under Preferences → Connections, or an organization admin disconnects it for them or for everyone, the user is deactivated or removed from the organization, or becomes a guest, an organization admin blocks your app for the user, for example by restricting it to Owners and admins, it expires, as described under Refreshing. Changing a password doesn't end connections.

Every approval creates its own connection, with its own tokens. Connecting the same app from a second device doesn't disconnect the first. A user can hold up to 10 connections to the same app, and an eleventh ends the oldest. A client Tape registered to keep one connection per user is the exception. There, each new sign-in replaces the user's previous connection, so store the newest tokens every time.

The token, revocation, and registration endpoints answer errors in the standard OAuth shape. error_description ends with a reason ID in brackets. Errors from the authorization endpoint carry the same reason IDs: in the redirect's error_description, on Tape's error page, or in a 400 JSON body. { "error": "invalid_grant", "error_description": "The authorization code is unknown or has expired. [TOKEN_CODE_UNKNOWN]" } Quote the reason ID when you contact Tape support. It names the exact cause. Status When 400 In general. 401 With invalid_client, when client authentication fails. 429 With temporarily_unavailable and a Retry-After header, when you are rate limited. The reason IDs you are most likely to meet: Reason ID Meaning AUTHORIZE_CLIENT_INVALID The client_id is missing, unknown or revoked. Tape removes a dynamically registered client that no user connected within 25 hours, and it lands here. Register again. AUTHORIZE_REDIRECT_URI_INVALID redirect_uri is missing or matches no registered URI. AUTHORIZE_CIMD_DOCUMENT_INVALID Tape couldn't fetch your client ID metadata document, or it is invalid. AUTHORIZE_PKCE_INVALID No code challenge, a method other than S256, or a malformed challenge. AUTHORIZE_SCOPE_UNKNOWN A requested scope doesn't exist. Check for typos, and separate scopes with single spaces. AUTHORIZE_RESOURCE_INVALID resource is neither https://api.tapeapp.com/v1 nor https://mcp.tapeapp.com/mcp. CLIENT_AUTH_FAILED Unknown client, wrong or missing secret, or a public client sending a secret. CLIENT_AUTH_AMBIGUOUS More than one client authentication method in one request. TOKEN_CODE_UNKNOWN The code expired (after 60 seconds) or was never issued. TOKEN_CODE_REPLAYED The code was used before. Tape disconnected its connection. TOKEN_CODE_BINDING_MISMATCH The code belongs to another client, or redirect_uri differs from the authorization request. TOKEN_PKCE_VERIFIER_PRESENCE / TOKEN_PKCE_VERIFIER_MISMATCH code_verifier is missing, or doesn't match the challenge. TOKEN_CODE_REDEMPTION_REFUSED The user can no longer connect your app: deactivated, a guest, or blocked by the organization's app settings. TOKEN_REFRESH_TOKEN_UNKNOWN Not a refresh token of this client. TOKEN_REFRESH_GRANT_INACTIVE The connection was disconnected or expired, or the organization now blocks your app. Start a new authorization. TOKEN_REFRESH_SCOPE_INVALID The refresh asked for a scope the connection doesn't hold. Nothing was used up. TOKEN_REFRESH_REPLAYED A public client re-sent a used refresh token too late or too often. Tape disconnected the connection.

The API answers in its own error format. An access token that is no longer valid gets the same 401, whatever the cause: expired, revoked, disconnected, or blocked by the organization. { "status_code": 401, "endpoint": "/v1/record/1", "error_code": "dev_api_invalid_access_token", "error_message": "Invalid access token for accessing endpoint '/v1/record/1' (the access token is not active)" } WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="https://api.tapeapp.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/v1", error="invalid_token", error_description="The access token is not active." Refresh the access token. If the refresh fails with invalid_grant, start a new authorization. A missing scope is a 403, covered under Asking for more scopes.

Tape follows OAuth 2.1 and the related RFCs, with these deliberate differences: One token for both Tape resources. Every access token is valid at the Developer API and the MCP server, whichever resource you asked for. redirect_uri is required in every authorization request, even with a single registered redirect URI. A missing code_challenge_method means S256, not plain. Revoking another client's token answers 200 and revokes nothing. Nobody can use the endpoint to find out whose token it is. Tape doesn't support private_key_jwt. Tape accepts a client ID metadata document that prefers it as a public client, if the document also lists none. Tape ignores jwks_uri. Tape can waive PKCE for a confidential client it registered, on request. A code issued without PKCE requires redirect_uri at the token endpoint.

Register a client get the client ID this flow needs. Integration guide run this flow safely from your backend. Capabilities pick the scopes to request in step 2. Errors read the error format of the Developer API. Request limits the budget connected apps share with the user. OAuth overview compare OAuth with personal access tokens.

Email team@tapeapp.com with: your app's name, a short description, and its website, its redirect URIs: the exact URLs Tape may send the user back to (see Redirect URIs), whether it has a backend that can keep a secret (a confidential client), or runs entirely on the user's device or in a browser (a public client), for a confidential client, whether your app keeps one connection per Tape user. With that setting, a new sign-in replaces the user's previous connection. This is usual for a "Sign in with Tape" backend. See the integration guide. You receive a client ID that starts with tape_oc_. A confidential client also gets a client secret that starts with tape_ocs_. Tape shares the secret only once Store the client secret in your backend's secret store. Never ship it in a browser, mobile, or desktop app.

The consent screen shows a client registered by Tape under your app's name. A confidential client's connections never reach an absolute expiry. An unattended sync keeps running as long as it refreshes at least once every 90 days. Rotating the client secret? When Tape rotates your client secret, the previous secret keeps working for a transition period: seven days, unless agreed otherwise. Deploy the new secret before the old one stops.

An MCP client or AI platform can't be registered by hand for every server it talks to. Self-registration lets it connect to the Tape MCP server without anyone setting it up first. Tape supports the two standard ways to do this. Both create a public client. A public client has no secret and proves possession with PKCE alone. Tape treats a client that registers itself as an MCP client: Its consent screen reads Connect with Tape MCP. Organization owners and admins manage it under Tape MCP in their settings.

With a client ID metadata document, the client ID is an https URL. That URL serves a JSON document that describes the client. Tape fetches the document the first time a user starts a sign-in, so there is no registration request at all. https://app.example.com/oauth/client-metadata.json { "client_id": "https://app.example.com/oauth/client-metadata.json", "client_name": "Example Assistant", "client_uri": "https://app.example.com", "redirect_uris": ["https://app.example.com/oauth/callback", "http://127.0.0.1/callback"], "grant_types": ["authorization_code", "refresh_token"], "response_types": ["code"], "token_endpoint_auth_method": "none" } Requirements​ The URL must: use https and have a path, contain no credentials or fragment, be in canonical form and at most 2048 characters long, have a domain name as its host, not an IP address, and name no port. The document must: name the URL itself as its client_id, list at least one redirect_uris entry, each one admissible, be a public client: token_endpoint_auth_method is none, or none appears in token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported, include authorization_code in grant_types, if grant_types is present. Tape ignores members it doesn't use. How Tape fetches the document​ Tape requests the document on port 443, follows no redirects, and waits at most 5 seconds. The response must be 200 OK with Content-Type: application/json, uncompressed, and at most 5 KB. Tape caches a document for up to an hour, so a change can take that long to apply. Your host is unreachable, times out, answers 5xx, 408 or 429, or returns something that isn't a JSON document of at most 5 KB? Tape keeps using the last good copy for up to a day. Your host answers any other 4xx, a redirect, or a document that breaks the rules above? Tape discards its copy. Sign-ins stop until the host serves a valid document again. On the consent screen​ The consent screen shows the app by its client ID URL, or by its own name if Tape recognizes it. Tape doesn't mark it Unverified, because the document's address shows who published it. The document's client_name doesn't appear.

A client can also register by posting its metadata to the registration endpoint. No authentication is needed. curl https://api.tapeapp.com/oauth/register \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "client_name": "Example Assistant", "redirect_uris": ["http://127.0.0.1/callback"] }' Response (201 Created) { "client_id": "tape_oc_8f14e45fceea167a5a36dedd4bea2543", "client_id_issued_at": 1791000000, "client_name": "Example Assistant", "redirect_uris": ["http://127.0.0.1/callback"], "grant_types": ["authorization_code", "refresh_token"], "response_types": ["code"], "token_endpoint_auth_method": "none" } The response echoes what Tape accepted. It can differ from what you sent: Public clients only. Tape issues no client secret and replaces any token_endpoint_auth_method with none. Redirect URIs are filtered. Tape drops inadmissible entries and echoes the rest. The request fails with invalid_redirect_uri only when none remain. Send at most 10 entries and 4096 characters in total. client_name is cut to 100 characters and defaults to the first redirect URI's host. Tape ignores logo_uri. It keeps client_uri only when it is an https URL, without credentials, on the host of one of your https redirect URIs. scope and grant_types never limit the client. You choose scopes per authorization request, and Tape issues a refresh token either way. Tape drops unsupported grant_types values. The request fails with invalid_client_metadata when: grant_types is present without authorization_code, response_types is anything other than ["code"], the redirect URIs exceed the limits above. General behavior​ Registration is idempotent for 24 hours. Posting identical metadata again returns the same client ID. Every installation that registers with the same metadata shares one client ID, so treat it as public. Unused registrations expire. Tape deletes a client that no user connected within 25 hours of registering, and eventually one whose connections have all ended. When the authorization endpoint then refuses your client ID with AUTHORIZE_CLIENT_INVALID, register again. A browser sees an error page, and a request that sends Accept: application/json gets a 400 with an invalid_client body. On the consent screen, a client whose redirect URIs are all https on one host appears under that host. Any other self-registered client, one that returns to a loopback address or a custom URL scheme, carries the badge Unverified.

The same rules apply to every kind of client. A redirect URI may be: Kind Example Notes https https://app.example.com/oauth/callback The usual choice for a web app. Loopback http http://127.0.0.1/callback Only on 127.0.0.1, [::1] or localhost. Any port matches, so register it without one. Private-use scheme com.example.app:/oauth/callback For desktop and mobile apps. Tape refuses javascript, data, file, blob and similar schemes. A redirect URI must contain no credentials and no fragment, be in canonical form, and be at most 2048 characters long. The authorization request's redirect_uri must match a registered one exactly, apart from a loopback URI's port.

The token and revocation endpoints identify the client in one of three ways. Use exactly one per request. Method For How client_secret_basic Confidential client HTTP Basic authentication, with the client ID as the username and the secret as the password. client_secret_post Confidential client client_id and client_secret in the form body. none Public client client_id in the form body. PKCE proves possession.

A confidential client may use either secret method, regardless of which one it registered. Tape refuses a secret sent both ways, or a body client_id that differs from the Basic username, with invalid_request. Tape treats a public client that sends Basic authentication with an empty password as none.

Authorization flow use your client ID to connect a user. Integration guide set up a confidential client for a "Sign in with Tape" backend. Connect to Tape MCP how MCP clients connect with a self-registered client. OAuth overview find every endpoint and credential format. Personal access tokens call the API from your own code without a client.

OAuth is mainly for MCP clients and for integrations and partners registered by Tape. You are building Use A script, internal tool or integration that calls the API directly, including on a user's behalf A personal access token An MCP client or AI platform OAuth, with a client that registers itself An integration or partner product with a "Connect to Tape" or "Sign in with Tape" button OAuth, with a client registered by Tape. See the integration guide A personal access token can do everything an OAuth token can do, and more. It needs no client registration, no redirect, no consent screen and no refreshing. You can limit it to selected workspaces and apps. See Which credential to use.

Your app sends the user's browser to Tape's authorization endpoint and names the scopes it needs. The user signs in to Tape if needed and chooses the organization to connect. The consent screen shows your app's name and what your app can do. The user approves. Tape redirects the browser back to your app with a short-lived authorization code. Your app exchanges the code at the token endpoint for an access token and a refresh token. Your app calls the API with the access token. The access token lasts one hour. Use the refresh token to get a new one. Each approval creates a connection between the user and your app. A connection keeps working until one of these happens: The user, an organization admin, or your app disconnects it. The user loses access to the organization. 90 days pass without a refresh. 365 days pass since the user approved it. This doesn't apply when Tape registered your client as a confidential one. The authorization flow walks through every step. Where do users see their connections? In Tape, users select their profile picture, then select Preferences → Connections. MCP clients appear under Tape MCP instead. Organization owners and admins manage connections for everyone on the Manage tab of the same pages.

Grant type Supported Authorization code with PKCE (authorization_code) Yes, the only way to get a token Refresh token (refresh_token) Yes Client credentials No Device authorization No Implicit, resource owner password No, OAuth 2.1 removes both PKCE is required, with the S256 method. Tape refuses plain. The response type is code, and the response mode is query. Tape is not an OpenID Connect provider. There is no id_token and no OpenID userinfo endpoint. The token response names the user (tape_user_id), and GET /v1/user returns the rest. Tokens are opaque. They are not JWTs. Don't try to decode them.

The issuer is https://api.tapeapp.com. Endpoint URL Authorization server metadata (RFC 8414) GET https://api.tapeapp.com/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server Authorization GET https://api.tapeapp.com/oauth/authorize Token POST https://api.tapeapp.com/oauth/token Revocation (RFC 7009) POST https://api.tapeapp.com/oauth/revoke Dynamic client registration (RFC 7591) POST https://api.tapeapp.com/oauth/register Protected resource metadata, Developer API GET https://api.tapeapp.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/v1 Protected resource metadata, Tape MCP GET https://mcp.tapeapp.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp The authorization server metadata also lists an introspection endpoint. Tape reserves it for its own services, and it refuses every other client. Discover the endpoints from the metadata instead of hard-coding them: GET https://api.tapeapp.com/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server { "issuer": "https://api.tapeapp.com", "authorization_endpoint": "https://api.tapeapp.com/oauth/authorize", "token_endpoint": "https://api.tapeapp.com/oauth/token", "revocation_endpoint": "https://api.tapeapp.com/oauth/revoke", "introspection_endpoint": "https://api.tapeapp.com/oauth/introspect", "registration_endpoint": "https://api.tapeapp.com/oauth/register", "scopes_supported": ["apps:read", "records:read"], "response_types_supported": ["code"], "response_modes_supported": ["query"], "grant_types_supported": ["authorization_code", "refresh_token"], "token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported": ["client_secret_basic", "client_secret_post", "none"], "revocation_endpoint_auth_methods_supported": ["client_secret_basic", "client_secret_post", "none"], "introspection_endpoint_auth_methods_supported": ["client_secret_basic", "client_secret_post"], "code_challenge_methods_supported": ["S256"], "client_id_metadata_document_supported": true, "authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported": true, "service_documentation": "https://developers.tapeapp.com/oauth" } scopes_supported lists only the default read scopes. You can request every scope in Capabilities.

The token and revocation endpoints take application/x-www-form-urlencoded bodies. Registration takes application/json. Send each parameter at most once. Only resource may repeat. The token, revocation, and registration endpoints and all three metadata documents allow cross-origin requests. An app that runs in a browser can call them.

It acts as the user. Its access is the user's own permissions, narrowed by the scopes the user approved. Records it creates or changes show the user as the author. It reaches everything the user can. Unlike a personal access token, you can't limit an OAuth access token to selected workspaces and apps. It works at the Developer API and the MCP server alike. One token is valid at https://api.tapeapp.com/v1 and at https://mcp.tapeapp.com/mcp. It shares the user's rate limit. Every connected app draws from the same per-user budget as the user's personal access tokens. See Request limits. Send it as a bearer token, the same way as a personal access token: curl https://api.tapeapp.com/v1/user \ -H "Authorization: Bearer tape_oat_0a1b2c3d..."
documents.s: What an access token can do

documents.t: Every OAuth credential has a recognizable prefix. The prefix is part of the value. Store and send each credential exactly as you received it. Credential Prefix Lifetime Access token tape_oat_ 1 hour Refresh token tape_ort_ Public client: single use, each refresh returns a new one. Confidential client: as long as its connection. See Refreshing Authorization code tape_oac_ 60 seconds, single use Client ID tape_oc_ None. A metadata document client uses its URL instead Client secret tape_ocs_ Until Tape rotates it

Register a client: get a client_id, and a secret if your app has a backend. Authorization flow: send each request step by step, then refresh, ask for more scopes, and disconnect. Integration guide: connect your product's users to Tape from your backend. Capabilities: every scope you can request. Personal access tokens: call the API directly without a client. Request limits: the per-user budget connected apps share. In the Help Center: Connect apps with OAuth 2.1

documents.s: Build a Tape integration with OAuth

documents.t: Ask Tape for a confidential client with exact https redirect URIs. Mention whether your app keeps one connection per Tape user. With that setting, a new sign-in replaces that Tape user's previous connection, even when it comes from a different account in your product. Two of your accounts linked to the same Tape user can't both stay connected. A confidential client registered by Tape has no yearly reconnect. Its connections last as long as you refresh them at least once every 90 days.

Start every sign-in from an endpoint on your backend: Create a fresh state and PKCE code_verifier. Use PKCE even though your client has a secret. Store both in a short-lived, HttpOnly, Secure cookie, set on the user's browser by this endpoint. Redirect the browser to the authorization endpoint, and request every scope your integration needs. Tape shows the consent screen on every sign-in, including when the user already approved your app. Bind the sign-in to the browser, not to state On the callback, read state and the verifier from the cookie, and compare. Never look up a pending sign-in by the state value alone. Otherwise an attacker can have their own sign-in completed in a victim's browser, which links the victim's Tape account to the attacker's account in your product.

Check state against the cookie, and iss against https://api.tapeapp.com. Exchange the code once. Never retry a code exchange: a code presented twice disconnects the connection it created. Key the account on tape_user_id from the token response, and store tape_organization_id beside it. A person who belongs to two Tape organizations is two Tape users, with two IDs. Read scope from the token response to learn what the user granted. Overwrite the stored token pair on every sign-in. If your client keeps one connection per user, the new sign-in replaced the old connection, and the old tokens stop working. Need the user's name, email, or organization name? Call GET /v1/user with the new access token.

Refresh when the access token expires, or when the API answers 401. A confidential client keeps the refresh token from the code exchange for the whole connection. Refresh responses contain no new refresh token, so don't overwrite the stored one with an empty value. Refresh at least once every 90 days, or the connection expires. On invalid_grant, re-read before giving up. Another sign-in may have replaced the stored tokens while your refresh was in flight. Re-read the stored pair, and retry once if it changed. Only when Tape refuses the current pair, mark the account as disconnected and ask the user to sign in again.

When the user disconnects Tape in your product, revoke the refresh token. That ends the connection in Tape as well, instead of leaving it to expire. Users can also disconnect your app in Tape, under Preferences → Connections. Your next refresh then fails with invalid_grant.

Tape is an OAuth 2.1 authorization server, not an OpenID Connect provider. It publishes an OAuth metadata document but no OpenID configuration, and issues no ID token. Configure libraries for plain OAuth.

{ id: 'tape', name: 'Tape', type: 'oauth', issuer: 'https://api.tapeapp.com', clientId: process.env.TAPE_CLIENT_ID, clientSecret: process.env.TAPE_CLIENT_SECRET, authorization: { url: 'https://api.tapeapp.com/oauth/authorize', params: { scope: 'apps:read records:read records:edit' }, }, token: 'https://api.tapeapp.com/oauth/token', userinfo: 'https://api.tapeapp.com/v1/user', checks: ['pkce', 'state'], profile(profile) { return { id: String(profile.user_id), name: profile.name, email: profile.email }; }, } Set issuer. Tape sends iss on the callback. Without a configured issuer, the check fails. Store the tokens on every sign-in. Auth.js doesn't update a stored account when the same user signs in again. Write the new token pair in the events.signIn callback. NextAuth v4 with the Prisma adapter writes every field of the token response to the account. Add tape_user_id Int? and tape_organization_id Int? to the Account model, or the first sign-in fails. Auth.js v5 stores only the standard token fields. To keep the Tape IDs, add the same two columns and return them from the provider's account(tokens) callback. Return the standard fields there too (access_token, refresh_token, expires_at, scope, token_type), because that callback replaces the default one. For a public client, set client: { token_endpoint_auth_method: 'none' }.

Discover the server as OAuth, not as OpenID Connect: import * as client from 'openid-client'; const config = await client.discovery( new URL('https://api.tapeapp.com'), process.env.TAPE_CLIENT_ID, process.env.TAPE_CLIENT_SECRET, undefined, { algorithm: 'oauth2' }, );

import base64, hashlib, os, secrets from requests_oauthlib import OAuth2Session os.environ['OAUTHLIB_RELAX_TOKEN_SCOPE'] = '1' def tape_session(state=None): return OAuth2Session( client_id, redirect_uri='https://app.example.com/oauth/callback', scope=['apps:read', 'records:read', 'records:edit'], state=state, ) # Start the sign-in verifier = secrets.token_urlsafe(64) challenge = base64.urlsafe_b64encode(hashlib.sha256(verifier.encode()).digest()).rstrip(b'=').decode() url, state = tape_session().authorization_url( 'https://api.tapeapp.com/oauth/authorize', code_challenge=challenge, code_challenge_method='S256', ) # Store state and verifier in the cookie, then redirect the browser to url. # On the callback, after checking state and iss: token = tape_session(state=state_from_cookie).fetch_token( 'https://api.tapeapp.com/oauth/token', authorization_response=callback_url, code_verifier=verifier_from_cookie, client_secret=client_secret, ) Set OAUTHLIB_RELAX_TOKEN_SCOPE. requests-oauthlib raises an error when the granted scopes differ from the requested ones, for example when Tape ignores a requested offline_access. It checks again on every refresh. Create the PKCE verifier yourself. The session's pkce= option keeps the verifier only on the session object that built the authorization URL. A callback handled in a separate request can't use it. Authenticate on refresh. refresh_token() sends no client credentials by default. Pass auth=(client_id, client_secret) for a confidential client, or client_id=client_id for a public one. You can also set them once in auto_refresh_kwargs. For a public client, pass include_client_id=True to fetch_token.

When a refresh fails with invalid_grant, the default failure handler of Spring Security removes the stored authorized client. That may be the newer one another sign-in stored a moment ago. Call OAuth2AuthorizedClientManager.authorize() without a pre-loaded authorized client, so it reads the current tokens before giving up.

Authorization flow look up every request and reason ID behind these steps. Register a client send Tape the details for your confidential client. Capabilities choose the scopes your integration requests. User get the name and email of a connected user. Request limits plan a sync within the user's per-user budget.

Cursor-paginated endpoints accept these parameters: Parameter Type Description cursor string (optional) A cursor from a previous response, used to request the next page. Treat it as opaque. Omit it (default) to start from the beginning. limit integer (optional) The maximum number of items to return in the page. The response may contain fewer. Defaults and maximums vary per endpoint. What are the default and maximum for limit? 50 / 500 is the common case, for example for the record listing and filter endpoints and the automation run endpoints. It isn't universal: record comments cap at 100, and related records default to 1000. Each endpoint page states its own default and maximum. Where do the parameters go? For GET endpoints, pass cursor and limit in the query string. For POST endpoints, pass them in the request body. The exception: the record filter endpoint uses POST but reads cursor and limit from the query string. The related records endpoint reads only limit there and has no pagination. When in doubt, follow the example on the endpoint's own page.

A cursor-paginated response contains these properties: Property Type Description total integer The number of items that match the request across all pages. Tape measures it when you request the first page. Treat it as an approximate snapshot, not a live count. cursor string An opaque cursor that points at the last item on this page. Pass it back as the cursor parameter to fetch the next page. Some endpoints return null at the end. collection array The page of results. The property is named for the resource, such as records, comments or automation_runs. It's not a generic results. A response looks like this (here the collection is records): { "total": 128, "cursor": "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9...", "records": [ { "record_id": 2 }, { "record_id": 3 } ] } For example, request the next page of records of a database app with GET /v1/record/app/1?limit=50&cursor=eyJhbGci....

Repeat the request with the cursor from the previous response until a page has fewer items than limit, or cursor is null. Without limit, compare with the endpoint's default. Paging search or shared records? Several endpoints return a cursor even on the last page, so a short page marks the end. Search and shared records are the exception: page them until cursor is null. A full page can be the last one, and a search page can be short and still not be the last.

Some endpoints return their entire collection in one response and accept no cursor or limit. They typically return { "total": <n>, "<collection>": [ ... ] }, and sometimes only the array. Their resource pages document this. Don't assume a collection endpoint is pageable unless its page documents cursor and limit.
Record list and filter records page by page. Request limits the request budget behind every page. Errors handle error responses.

Select your profile picture, then select Preferences. In the settings window, select Developer (under Features). Under Personal access tokens (PATs), select New token. Enter a Token name, for example "Monthly sales report". Under Content access, keep All or select only the workspaces and apps the integration needs. Under Capabilities, keep All or select only what the integration needs, for example Read records. Select Create token and copy the token. Tape shows the token only once Copy the token right away and store it in a safe place, such as your integration's secret store. Tape keeps only a hash, so it can't show the value again. If you lose it, revoke the token and create a new one. The token list then shows only the first and last few characters of each token. Need different capabilities or content access? You can rename a token later. To change its capabilities or content access, create a new token and revoke the old one.

Send the token as a bearer token, the same way as a user API key: curl https://api.tapeapp.com/v1/record/1 \ -H "Authorization: Bearer tape_pat_0a1b2c3d..." A personal access token works for the Developer API (/v1/*) only. It can't create or manage personal access tokens; you do that in Tape while signed in.

When you create a token, you choose its reach: Content access What the token can reach All Every workspace and app you can reach, including ones created later. Only some Clear All and select the workspaces and apps the token may reach. A selected workspace includes every app in it, also apps added later. A selected app does not include its workspace. See Limits for how many you can select.

A request for a resource outside the token's content access returns 404, as if the resource didn't exist. List endpoints return 200 with fewer results. This applies to GET /v1/app, GET /v1/workspace/org, GET /v1/automation/org, the automation run history, and search. Some endpoints name the resource in the request body: workspace_id when you create an app, record_ids when you batch-update record permissions, and trigger_workflow_def_id when you generate an automation weblink. Tape checks these against the token's content access too. Creating a workspace requires a token with All. A new top-level workspace has no parent that content access could name. Content access limits a credential, not your data Content access doesn't isolate data, hide data from you, or change anyone's permissions. Related records of a record in a selected app come back as read-only previews (ID, title, creation date, app, and workspace), even from apps the token didn't select. The previews stay within your own permissions.

Revoke a token in the same Developer section. Revocation applies from the next request on. Revoking one token doesn't affect your other tokens, your user API key, or your account. Revoked tokens stay in the list, so you keep a record of what existed. Webhooks outlive the token that created them A webhook created through the API keeps delivering after you revoke the token that created it. Delete those webhooks separately.
Limit Value Active tokens per user 20 Selected workspaces per token 50 Selected apps per token 50 Token name length 500 characters

A personal access token has no rate limit budget of its own. Your user API key, all your tokens and your OAuth connections share one per-user budget, so more tokens don't mean more throughput. See Request limits.

A token acts as you. Records it creates or changes show you as the author, and it sends emails on your behalf. To show an integration under its own name, create a dedicated user for it and create the token from that account.

Never commit a token to source control or put it in a client-side app. A token in a browser bundle is public. Use one token per integration, so you can revoke one without breaking another. Grant the fewest capabilities that work. A reporting integration needs only read capabilities. Select only the workspaces and apps the integration needs. Secret-scanning tools recognize the tape_pat_ prefix, so they can spot a leaked token. If a token may have leaked, revoke it first and investigate afterwards.

Quickstart: retrieve your first record with a token. Capabilities: the capability each endpoint needs. Request limits: the per-user budget all your tokens share. Authentication: compare tokens with OAuth and the user API key. In the Help Center: Personal access tokens

A rate-limited request returns HTTP status 429 with the error code user_too_many_requests. The base rate limit is an average of 3 requests per second. Short bursts above the average are allowed. Handle 429 responses and slow down your following requests. After a 429, wait the number of seconds in the Retry-After header before you retry. A common pattern is one or more queues for pending requests. Keep sending from the queue as long as Tape doesn't respond with 429. Rate limits may change Tape plans to adjust rate limits to balance demand and reliability. Tape may also introduce distinct rate limits for organizations on different pricing plans.

Tape enforces rate limits with credits: Each user has 2,000 credits per minute. After the minute, the credits refill. A request costs 10 credits by default. Expensive requests cost more, for example creating a record or creating, updating or deleting an app. Some endpoint pages list their cost. The X-Retry-Cost header shows the cost of every request. All credentials of a user share the same budget: the user API key, every personal access token they own, and every app or MCP client they connected with OAuth. More tokens don't mean more throughput. A request that authenticates but lacks a capability, or falls outside a token's content access, still costs credits. Tape checks both after rate limiting. Coming from the Podio API? Tape counts credits per minute, not calls per hour.

Tape sends rate limit headers with every response. Use them to slow down before you hit the limit. These are the response headers of a valid request: HTTP/1.1 200 OK Retry-After: 57 X-RateLimit-Limit: 2000 X-Retry-Remaining: 1990 X-Retry-Cost: 10 X-Retry-Reset: 2022-03-01 12:00:00 X-RateLimit-Scope: user HTTP header Description Example X-RateLimit-Limit Total credits per time interval. 2000 X-Retry-Remaining Credits left in this time interval. 1980 X-Retry-Cost Credits the current request used. 10 X-Retry-Reset Date and time at which the credits reset. 2022-03-01 12:00:00 Retry-After Seconds left in this interval until the credits reset. 60 X-RateLimit-Scope Which budget the request counts against: user for a user's credentials, workflow for an automation API key. user Which timezone does X-Retry-Reset use? X-Retry-Reset uses the format YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm:ss, the same datetime format as the rest of the API, with no Z suffix and no numeric offset. Unlike the temporal properties in response bodies, it's a header and has no local counterpart: it's in UTC. See Date & timezone. When you exceed the rate limit, the error response body also contains all rate limit information: { "status_code": 429, "endpoint": "/v1/record/123", "error_code": "user_too_many_requests", "error_message": "Too many requests (0/2000 credits left) for user with ID 1, retry after 58 seconds (2022-03-01 12:00:00). Your current request costs 10 credits. Check https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/request-limits for more info", "retry_after": 58, "rate_limit": 2000, "rate_limit_remaining": 0, "rate_limit_cost": 10, "rate_limit_reset": "2022-03-01 12:00:00" }

Avoid API requests inside loops. Load a collection of objects in one request instead of one object per request. Cache results where you can. Don't poll for changed data. Use webhooks to react to changes. Log your requests to see how many you make.
Need more credits per time interval, for example for a large partner integration? Ask the Tape team to raise your limit.

Tape limits the size of some parameters. A request above a limit returns HTTP status 400 with the error code validation. The error_message property says which limit applies. Stay below the size limits in your integration. Add test data with deliberately large parameters to your test suite to check that you handle the errors.
