Errors handle 401, 403 and 429 responses. Automations run your own JavaScript inside Tape.

You need: A personal access token with the capabilities Manage webhooks (webhooks:manage) and Read records (records:read). Add Edit records (records:edit) if your handler changes records. The ID of the app you want to watch. Open one of its records in Tape, select •••, then select Developer, and copy the App ID. A record you read with the API also returns it as app_id. The Admin role in the app's workspace. Node.js 18 or later, and the Express package (npm install express). Store the token in an environment variable: export TAPE_TOKEN=tape_pat_0a1b2c3d...

You create a webhook with a URL and an event type. It starts as inactive. Tape sends hook.verify with a code to your URL right away. Your handler sends the code back to Tape. The webhook becomes active. From then on, Tape sends one POST request per event to your URL. Every event carries IDs only, for example record_id and revision_id. Read the record with your token to get its values.

Create server.js: server.js const express = require('express'); const TAPE_API = 'https://api.tapeapp.com'; const headers = { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.TAPE_TOKEN}`, 'Content-Type': 'application/json', }; const app = express(); app.use(express.json()); app.post('/tape-webhook', async (req, res) => { // Answer first. Tape waits 5 seconds at most. res.sendStatus(200); const { type, hook_id, code, record_id } = req.body; if (type === 'hook.verify') { await fetch(`${TAPE_API}/v1/hook/${hook_id}/verify/validate`, { method: 'POST', headers, body: JSON.stringify({ code }), }); console.log(`Webhook ${hook_id} verified`); return; } if (type === 'record.update') { const record = await fetch(`${TAPE_API}/v1/record/${record_id}`, { headers }).then((r) => r.json()); console.log(`Record ${record_id} updated: ${record.title}`); } }); app.listen(3000, () => console.log('Listening on port 3000')); Start it: node server.js Key points res.sendStatus(200) comes first. Slow work after the response doesn't count against the time limit. The handler validates the code itself, so verification needs no manual step. Tape doesn't sign webhook requests, so the handler reads the record with your token. Don't trust the payload for anything but IDs.

Tape sends webhooks only to ports 80 and 443. A server on localhost:3000 isn't reachable from the internet. To test on your machine, start a tunnel such as ngrok or Cloudflare Tunnel. It forwards a public HTTPS URL on port 443 to your local port: ngrok http 3000 Copy the HTTPS URL it prints, for example https://acme-test.ngrok.app. Your webhook URL is that address plus /tape-webhook. In production, run the handler behind HTTPS on port 443. Tape sends the same payload over HTTP, but HTTPS keeps it private.

Keep the handler and the tunnel running. Make a POST request with the URL and the event type. Replace 1 in the path with your app ID: curl -X POST https://api.tapeapp.com/v1/hook/app/1 \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TAPE_TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ --data '{ "type": "record.update", "url": "https://acme-test.ngrok.app/tape-webhook" }' Response { "hook_id": 7, "app_id": 1, "status": "inactive", "num_failed_executions": 0, "type": "record.update", "url": "https://acme-test.ngrok.app/tape-webhook" } One webhook receives one event type. To receive created and updated records, create two webhooks with the same URL.

Your handler received hook.verify right after Step 3 and logs Webhook 7 verified. Check the status, again with your app ID in place of 1: curl https://api.tapeapp.com/v1/hook/app/1 \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TAPE_TOKEN" The webhook now shows "status": "active". Still inactive? Check that the tunnel runs, that the URL ends with /tape-webhook, and that your handler answers within 5 seconds. Then request the verification again with the hook_id from the response: curl -X POST https://api.tapeapp.com/v1/hook/7/verify/request \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TAPE_TOKEN"

Change any field of a record in that database app, in Tape or with Update a record. Tape sends this body to your handler: Incoming request { "hook_id": 7, "record_id": 100, "revision_id": 1, "type": "record.update" } Your handler logs the update: Record 100 updated: Andrea Lim

A handler that updates a record in the same app starts a new record.update event. That event calls the handler again, and the loop never ends. Add hook=false to every request your handler sends to change records. In this example, status is the slug of a field in the app: await fetch(`${TAPE_API}/v1/record/${record_id}?hook=false&silent=true`, { method: 'PUT', headers, body: JSON.stringify({ fields: { status: 'Reviewed' } }), }); hook=false runs no webhooks for this change. It works on create, update, delete, restore and the batch endpoints. silent=true sends no notifications for this change. workflow=false also skips automations, if one of them reacts to the same field.

Respond to every webhook request with a 2xx status code within 5 seconds: After more than 50 failed requests in a row, the webhook becomes inactive. Request the verification again to activate it. Tape retries a request briefly after a timeout, a network error, a 429 or a 5xx response. Other status codes fail at once. Tape doesn't follow redirects. Use the final URL, including https. Send an empty body or a short one, such as OK. A long body, such as an HTML page, counts as a failed request. The same event can arrive more than once. Use record_id and revision_id to skip events you already handled. Tape sends at most 100 webhook requests per minute per app.

Webhook every endpoint and event type. Record read and update the record of an event. Coming from the Podio API move existing Podio hooks to Tape. Request limits plan the requests your handler sends. Automations react to changes inside Tape without your own server.

Automations where scripts run and what they can do. Convert a PDF file to text extract text from an attached file. Connect Google Forms to Tape create a record for each form response. Connect Jotform to Tape receive Jotform submissions with a webhook.

documents.s: Convert a PDF file to text

documents.t: The automation has these steps: When a record is created: the automation starts when someone creates a task record. Filter: it continues only if the task's attachment field is not empty. In the screenshot, that field is PDF output, so the filter reads PDF output Is not empty. Execute a script: a script sends the attached file to a conversion API with the http.upload function. The script decodes the base64 response with Buffer.from and stores the result in the custom variable PDF plaintext. Update the current record: the automation writes the PDF plaintext variable to a text field of the task, such as its description. In the screenshot, that field is Note. Steps 3 and 4 need two statements: const { data } = await http.upload( 'https://v2.convertapi.com/convert/pdf/to/txt?Secret=YOUR_SECRET_HERE', task_field_attachment_file_url ); var_pdf_plaintext = Buffer.from(data.Files[0].FileData, 'base64'); Replace YOUR_SECRET_HERE with the secret of your ConvertAPI account. http.upload downloads the file from the URL in its second argument and posts it as the form field file. var_pdf_plaintext is the custom variable of the action, named after its label. The finished automation looks like this: The name of the file URL variable depends on your app and its attachment field. The code above uses task_field_attachment_file_url; the app and field in the screenshot give hc_test_task_field_pdf_output_file_url. The editor's autocompletion lists the variables of your app. The same approach works for other file formats, such as Word documents or PowerPoint presentations. To process the extracted text further, add a conditional action, for example one that assigns a user based on a keyword: "When the PDF contains the word 'legal', assign Juliet."
Create a task with a PDF attached. After the run, the text of the PDF is in the field you chose in step 5.
Automations where scripts run and what they can do. Automation showcase more examples with code. Field value the value format of every field type.

documents.s: Build an MCP client for Tape

documents.t: Requirement What Tape uses Endpoint https://mcp.tapeapp.com/mcp Transport Streamable HTTP: JSON-RPC 2.0 over POST. There is no SSE endpoint Authorization OAuth 2.1 authorization code flow with PKCE (S256), the only supported flow Discovery Protected resource metadata (RFC 9728), then authorization server metadata (RFC 8414) Client registration A client ID metadata document or dynamic client registration (RFC 7591) Credential A bearer access token on every request, renewed with a refresh token

Discover. Without a token, Tape answers initialize and every tool call with 401 and points to its protected resource metadata. Only tools/list, resources/* and ping work without a token. The metadata names Tape's authorization server and the scopes the Tape MCP tools use. Register as a public client. See Register a client yourself. Authorize with PKCE and request the scopes from the protected resource metadata. The user signs in to Tape and approves. See the authorization flow. Call tools with the access token, and refresh it when it expires. Step up when a tool needs a scope the connection lacks. Tape answers 403 and names the scopes to request. See Asking for more scopes. Capabilities describes each scope. The same access token also works at the Developer API. Can't run OAuth in your client? Send a personal access token as the bearer token instead.

OAuth overview the endpoints, supported flows and token formats. Register a client set up metadata documents, dynamic registration and redirect URIs. Authorization flow every request, refreshing, step-up and errors. Connect to Tape MCP what signing in looks like for a user, and how to troubleshoot it. Supported tools what each tool does and which capability it needs.

Use this in claude.ai, Claude Desktop and the Claude mobile apps. They share your connectors. Client documentation: Custom connectors using remote MCP. In Claude, open Customize → Connectors, select + Add, then Add custom connector. Name it Tape and enter https://mcp.tapeapp.com/mcp as the URL. If the dialog shows Advanced settings, leave them empty. If it asks you to review authentication settings instead, keep the recommended sign-in options and leave Request headers empty. Select Add, then Connect, and approve the connection in Tape. On Claude's Team and Enterprise plans, members can't add a custom connector themselves. An owner adds Tape for the whole organization under Organization settings → Connectors, with the same name and URL. Members then select Connect under Customize → Connectors and sign in with their own Tape account. To change a connector's settings later, remove it and add it again. Using Claude Desktop with a third-party model provider? On these deployments, members can't add connectors themselves. The deployment's admin adds Tape as a managed MCP server with OAuth turned on (extensions and MCP servers); each member then connects it and approves the connection in Tape. If Claude refuses the sign-in on the way back, the admin adds tapeapp.com to that server's oauth.additionalRedirectReferrerHosts.

Client documentation: Claude Code MCP. Add the server: claude mcp add --transport http tape https://mcp.tapeapp.com/mcp In Claude Code, run /mcp, select tape and choose Authenticate. Approve the connection in the browser window that opens. Options for claude mcp add: --scope user makes the server available in every project. --scope project writes it into the repository's .mcp.json so your team shares it. Each teammate signs in with their own Tape account. --callback-port is needed only if something on your machine requires a fixed port. Claude Code receives the sign-in on a random local port, and Tape accepts any port.

Client documentation: Add a custom MCP server. In ChatGPT on the web, go to Plugins, select the plus button, then Add custom MCP server. Name it Tape. Under Connection, enter https://mcp.tapeapp.com/mcp as the Server URL and choose OAuth authentication. Review the warning, select I understand and want to continue, then Create as a plugin. Install the plugin, then sign in and approve the connection in Tape. Your ChatGPT workspace permissions and security settings decide whether you can add and use custom MCP servers.

Client documentation: Cursor MCP. Create .cursor/mcp.json in your project with the content below. To use Tape in every project, create ~/.cursor/mcp.json instead. .cursor/mcp.json { "mcpServers": { "tape": { "url": "https://mcp.tapeapp.com/mcp" } } } Save the file and restart Cursor. Open Customize in the sidebar → MCPs, find Tape, follow the sign-in prompt, and approve the connection in Tape.

Client documentation: VS Code MCP servers. Create .vscode/mcp.json in your workspace with: .vscode/mcp.json { "servers": { "tape": { "type": "http", "url": "https://mcp.tapeapp.com/mcp" } } } VS Code uses servers where most clients use mcpServers, and it needs "type": "http". Open the Command Palette (Cmd+Shift+P / Ctrl+Shift+P), run MCP: List Servers, and start tape. Allow VS Code to sign in when it asks, and approve the connection in Tape. To use Tape in every workspace, run MCP: Open User Configuration and add the same entry there.

Client documentation: Codex MCP. Add the server to ~/.codex/config.toml, or to .codex/config.toml in a trusted project: ~/.codex/config.toml [mcp_servers.tape] url = "https://mcp.tapeapp.com/mcp" Sign in: codex mcp login tape Approve the connection in the browser window that opens.

Client documentation: Set up a custom MCP server. Gemini Enterprise doesn't discover Tape's sign-in by itself. A Google admin sets up the connection once, with a client ID and secret that Tape issues for your organization. Email team@tapeapp.com to request a Gemini Enterprise client for your Tape organization. Say whether you use Gemini Enterprise in the Google Cloud console or Gemini Business. In Gemini Enterprise, add a custom MCP server with OAuth 2.0 authentication: Field Value MCP Server URL https://mcp.tapeapp.com/mcp Authorization URL https://api.tapeapp.com/oauth/authorize Token URL https://api.tapeapp.com/oauth/token Client ID The client ID Tape sent you Client Secret The client secret Tape sent you Scopes See below In the Google Cloud console, also select Enable PKCE Support. In the Google Cloud console, wait until the data store is active. Then connect it to your Gemini Enterprise app. The admin, then each user, authorizes the connector once in the Gemini Enterprise web app and approves the connection in Tape. Only then, in the Google Cloud console, open the data store and select Actions → Reload custom actions. Select the Tape tools and select Enable actions. No action is enabled by default. Gemini can't ask for more scopes later, so the scopes you enter are all it ever gets. Fill them in even where the form marks the field optional; left empty, the connector can only read apps and records. For the full set of Tape MCP tools, enter them on one line, separated by single spaces: organization:read workspaces:read workspaces:edit apps:read apps:edit records:read records:edit records.comments:read records.comments:edit automations:read automations:edit automations:run Leave out automations:run if Gemini shouldn't start automations. It's the one capability whose effects can leave Tape. For a read-only connector: organization:read workspaces:read apps:read records:read records.comments:read automations:read Keep these points in mind: Google Cloud console prerequisites. The admin needs Google's Discovery Engine Editor role. The organization policy must allow custom MCP data stores, and the egress hosts mcp.tapeapp.com and api.tapeapp.com must be allowed. Users need Google Identity (Google Workspace or Cloud Identity) or workforce identity federation. See Google's guide. Gemini Business can't edit a connector's OAuth settings afterwards. To change them, delete the connector and create it again. No yearly reconnect. Connections through the client Tape issued last as long as Gemini uses them at least once every 90 days.

Any client that supports remote MCP servers with OAuth can connect. Add a Streamable HTTP server with Tape's URL, and complete the sign-in when the client asks: { "mcpServers": { "tape": { "url": "https://mcp.tapeapp.com/mcp" } } } Tape has no SSE endpoint. Wherever a client offers a transport, choose Streamable HTTP or plain "HTTP". In Tape, select your profile picture, then select Preferences → Tape MCP. Select Add an MCP client to see the URL there too. Clients that only run local servers reach Tape through the mcp-remote bridge. This includes Claude Desktop's claude_desktop_config.json. The bridge runs on your computer, opens the sign-in in your browser, and needs Node.js. { "mcpServers": { "tape": { "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "mcp-remote", "https://mcp.tapeapp.com/mcp"] } } } If the client can't sign in to remote servers either way, connect it with a token. To test the endpoint by hand, point the MCP Inspector at https://mcp.tapeapp.com/mcp and use its OAuth flow. Building your own client? See Build an MCP client.

Ask the assistant which Tape tools it has. A populated tool list shows that the client reaches the server. Ask it which Tape account it's connected as, for example "Which Tape user and organization are you connected as?" The answer names your user and your organization. The second step uses tape-fetch with type: "self", which needs no capability and also lists which tools the connection can use. If the tool list appears and this step fails, the problem is the sign-in, not the connection. tape-get-users is a different tool: it finds other people by name. From the shell, the health endpoint answers without any client: curl https://mcp.tapeapp.com/health Response { "status": "ok" }

Your client contacts the Tape MCP server and learns that it needs to sign in. It finds Tape's sign-in by itself. You only give it the server URL. Your browser opens Tape. Sign in if you aren't signed in yet. If you belong to more than one organization, choose the one to connect; the connection reaches only that one. For another organization, connect again, in most clients by adding Tape a second time under another name. Review the connection. The screen reads Connect with Tape MCP. It says that the client respects your Tape permissions, acts on your behalf, and can: View your organization and its members Run your automations, which can send emails and call other services This short list stands for every capability the Tape MCP tools use. A client that asks for a different set sees one line for each capability instead, for example a Gemini Enterprise connector set up with the read-only scopes. Tape marks a client Unverified when it can't tie the client to a website, typically a self-registered client on your own computer. The screen doesn't show where your browser returns to. Continue only if you started the connection yourself from the client. Select Continue. Your browser returns to the client, and the Tape tools are ready to use. The connection acts as you: it reaches only what you can reach in Tape, and everything it changes shows you as the author. One sign-in covers every capability the Tape MCP tools use. None of them manages members, shares records, manages webhooks or sends email; for a narrower connection, use a token. Who can connect. Every member of a Tape organization can connect a client. Guests can't. Owners and admins of an organization can also limit which clients members may connect. If your organization does, the sign-in screen tells you why it can't continue. How long it lasts. Your client renews its access in the background. A connection ends after 90 days unused, and one year after you approved it; the client then asks you to sign in again. Gemini Enterprise connections have no one-year limit. Each client and each device gets its own connection, so connecting a second laptop doesn't disconnect the first. You can hold up to 10 connections to the same client; an eleventh ends the oldest.

In Tape, select your profile picture, then select Preferences → Tape MCP → Connected. The list shows each MCP client you connected, when you first connected it, and when it was last used. Tape lists clients by app: Claude covers claude.ai, Claude Desktop and Claude Code. To disconnect a client on every device, select it and select Remove. It stops working on its next request. In the client, removing the server or connector deletes the client's copy of your sign-in. Most clients don't tell Tape, so the connection stays listed in Tape until it expires after 90 days unused. Remove it in Tape as well to end it right away.

Owners and admins manage clients for the whole organization under Tape MCP → Manage. There you choose which clients members can connect. Select All MCP clients to see every client; the per-client controls are in the ⋯ menu of a client's row. Which clients members can connect: All MCP clients or Approved MCP clients only. Switching to Approved MCP clients only disconnects no one. Tape approves every MCP client that someone in your organization is connected to at that moment. Review the Approved MCP clients list afterwards, and remove or restrict what you don't want. Removing a client from that list disconnects everyone from it. From then on, members can connect approved clients only. Owners and admins can connect any client. When only approved clients are allowed, connecting a client approves it for the organization. Limiting clients requires the Premium or Enterprise plan. In the ⋯ menu of a client's row: Access → Owners and admins: take a client away from members. The table then shows it as Restricted. Members' connections to it end immediately, and setting Access back to Everyone doesn't restore them. View members: see who connected a client, and disconnect one of them. Disconnect all members: disconnect everyone from one client, owners and admins included. To disconnect everyone from Tape MCP at once, select Disconnect all users. These controls apply to signed-in clients. A member can still connect a client with a personal access token.

The browser says Tape doesn't know the client registration. Tape removes a self-registered client if no one connects it within 25 hours. Remove Tape from the client and add it again. For mcp-remote, also delete its stored registrations with rm -rf ~/.mcp-auth. In VS Code, run Authentication: Remove Dynamic Authentication Providers, select Tape, and connect again. For Gemini Enterprise, the message means the client ID is wrong or no longer valid. Check it, or ask Tape for a new client. The sign-in page says "This request has expired". Complete a sign-in soon after you start it, in the browser where the sign-in page first opened. The page also shows this message when the request was already answered, for example after you went back in the browser, or when you opened its address in another browser. Start the connection again from your client and complete it in one browser. The sign-in page doesn't let you continue. It names the reason: guests can't connect clients, your organization allows only approved clients, or it limits this client to owners and admins. Ask an owner or admin of your organization. The sign-in page says the connection couldn't be completed, with reason AUTHORIZE_SCOPE_UNKNOWN. A scope is misspelled or contains an invisible character. This happens when you type scopes by hand, as in Gemini Enterprise. Recreate the connector with the one-line list under Gemini Enterprise. The client keeps asking you to approve more access. A connection with fewer scopes asks again the first time a tool needs one it lacks. Approve it, and the client continues with a new connection that includes it. It worked, and now Tape refuses every call with 401. The connection has ended: you or an admin removed it in Tape, it expired, or your role changed. Sign in again from the client. Calls fail with 503 and a Retry-After header. Tape couldn't check the connection at that moment. Wait a few seconds and retry. Your connection is unaffected. The client shows the server as failed, or reports an HTML or 405 error. The URL probably lacks the /mcp path, or the client is configured for SSE. Tape serves JSON-RPC over POST at https://mcp.tapeapp.com/mcp and answers every other method with 405. Opening that URL in a browser returns 405 by design. A tool returns 403 that names no capability. Then the connection's capabilities aren't the cause. Your own access applies, and a connection never grants access you don't have. Some actions require a role: creating a workspace requires an organization role that permits it, and changing a workspace requires the Admin role in the workspace. Reading a workspace returns no apps. Reading a workspace also returns its apps, which need apps:read on top of workspaces:read. Without it, you get the workspace back with apps: null and a reason, not an error. That null means Tape didn't read the apps at all, unlike [] (none you can see), so never report such a workspace as empty. A tool returns 404 for a record, app or automation you know exists. Tape answers 404 on purpose, the same as for a resource that doesn't exist. Check that your Tape user can see the resource; with a token, also check its content access. For an automation, every automation route also requires the Admin role in the app's workspace. Requests start failing with 429. All your connections and tokens share one per-user Developer API budget, so a busy assistant competes with your other integrations that use your tokens or user API key. Using Tape in the browser doesn't count against it. See Request limits. Tape rejects large tool arguments. Request bodies are capped at 128 KB. Split the work across several calls.

Can I connect without signing in through a browser? Yes. Connect with a personal access token. A token is also the way to give an assistant read-only access, or access to only some of your workspaces and apps. Can the assistant delete anything? No. No tool removes a record, comment, app, workspace, automation, field or field option, and none is planned; a person removes them in the Tape app. A write can still overwrite: tape-update-database replaces a field's configuration as a whole, so Tape flags it as destructive even though it deletes nothing. This limit applies to the tools, not to the credential. Most :edit capabilities permit deletion through any other client or script that uses the credential: records:edit covers deleting records. apps:edit covers deleting apps, fields and views. records.comments:edit covers deleting your own comments. automations:edit covers deleting automations. workspaces:edit covers deleting a workspace and everything inside it. The access token a client receives when you sign in is also valid at the Tape Developer API. How do I attach a file? In two steps: tape-create-file-upload creates a short-lived upload URL, then the client POSTs the file to it directly, so the bytes never travel through the MCP server. The handle you get back goes into an attachment or image field like any other value. A client that can't make HTTP requests of its own can't perform the second step; add the file in the Tape web interface instead. Do the assistant's writes trigger automations and webhooks? Yes, by default. A record or comment written through MCP behaves like one written by hand: it notifies followers, fires webhooks, and triggers automations, which can send email and make outbound HTTP calls. tape-create-records, tape-update-record and tape-create-comment accept silent, no_webhook and no_workflow to suppress each of these; all three default to false. See Security best practices.

Connect with a token: connect with narrower access through a personal access token. Supported tools: what each tool does and which capability it needs. Security best practices: what a connection can reach, and how to limit it. Capabilities: how capabilities limit a connection. Request limits: the shared per-user budget. Build an MCP client: build your own client. In the Help Center: Set up Tape MCP

documents.s: Connect with a personal access token

documents.t: Situation Why a token The assistant should reach only some workspaces or apps You can limit a token to selected workspaces and apps. A sign-in reaches everything you can The assistant should be read-only, or hold fewer capabilities You pick a token's capabilities one by one. A sign-in grants every capability the Tape MCP tools use It runs without a browser, for example on a server, in a CI job, or through the Claude API Signing in needs a person at a browser. You configure a token once The client can't sign in to remote MCP servers A token only needs the client to send a header, or the mcp-remote bridge Guests can't connect an MCP client either way. They can't sign in from a client, and they can't create a personal access token. A token created before someone became a guest stops working until they're a member again. A token connection and a signed-in connection see the same tools. A token limits them to the capabilities and content access you chose. When a capability is missing, a tool on a token fails and you create a new token; on a sign-in, your client asks you to approve more access.

Create a token for this client as described in Create a token: select your profile picture, then select Preferences → Developer → New token. The token sets what the connection may do and reach. Token name: for example "Read-only assistant". Content access: keep All or select only the workspaces and apps the assistant may reach. Capabilities: clear All, then select only what the assistant needs. For a read-only assistant, that's Read apps and Read records (apps:read, records:read). For more, see Choose capabilities. Select Create token and copy the token. Tape shows it only once. Treat the token like a password Keep the token out of the config file: use the environment variable or secret prompt shown for your client. Never commit a config file that contains a token, and revoke the token if it may have leaked.
Pick your client below. Each one sends the token in the Authorization header.
documents.s: Step 2: Add Tape to your client

documents.t: Client documentation: Claude Code MCP. claude mcp add --transport http tape https://mcp.tapeapp.com/mcp \ --header "Authorization: Bearer tape_pat_0a1b2c3d..." Add --scope user to make the server available in every project. Add --scope project to write it into the repository's .mcp.json. Since your team shares that file, use an environment variable there instead of the token itself.

Client documentation: Cursor MCP. Create .cursor/mcp.json in your project, or ~/.cursor/mcp.json to use Tape in every project. Paste the configuration below. Set TAPE_PAT in your shell profile instead of writing the token into the file. Save and restart Cursor. Tape then appears under Customize → MCPs. .cursor/mcp.json { "mcpServers": { "tape": { "url": "https://mcp.tapeapp.com/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${env:TAPE_PAT}" } } } }

Client documentation: VS Code MCP servers. Create .vscode/mcp.json in the workspace and paste the configuration below. The inputs block makes VS Code prompt for the token once and store it securely, so no secret goes into the file. Open the Command Palette (Cmd+Shift+P / Ctrl+Shift+P) and run MCP: List Servers. Start the Tape server. VS Code prompts for the token on first use. .vscode/mcp.json { "inputs": [ { "type": "promptString", "id": "tape-pat", "description": "Tape personal access token", "password": true } ], "servers": { "tape": { "type": "http", "url": "https://mcp.tapeapp.com/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${input:tape-pat}" } } } }

Custom connectors in Claude Desktop and on claude.ai normally connect by signing in. To use a token instead and keep it on your own machine, bridge to the endpoint with mcp-remote. It runs locally over stdio and forwards to the HTTP endpoint with your header. Add the configuration below to your claude_desktop_config.json. Restart Claude Desktop. claude_desktop_config.json { "mcpServers": { "tape": { "command": "npx", "args": [ "-y", "mcp-remote", "https://mcp.tapeapp.com/mcp", "--transport", "http-only", "--header", "Authorization:${TAPE_AUTH_HEADER}" ], "env": { "TAPE_AUTH_HEADER": "Bearer tape_pat_0a1b2c3d..." } } } } Two details in this snippet are deliberate: --transport http-only. Tape speaks Streamable HTTP and has no SSE endpoint, so the default SSE fallback finds nothing. Authorization:${TAPE_AUTH_HEADER} with no space, and Bearer inside the variable. Claude Desktop on Windows and Cursor break arguments that contain spaces. Keeping the space inside the environment variable avoids this. On macOS and Linux, you can write "Authorization: Bearer ${TAPE_PAT}" directly. The same configuration works in any other stdio-only client.

Client documentation: Windsurf MCP. Open Settings → Cascade → MCP servers → View raw config. This opens ~/.codeium/windsurf/mcp_config.json. Add the configuration below. Set TAPE_PAT in your shell profile. Save and restart Windsurf. mcp_config.json { "mcpServers": { "tape": { "serverUrl": "https://mcp.tapeapp.com/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${env:TAPE_PAT}" } } } } The header name must be exactly Authorization. The value must be Bearer followed by the token, with the space.

Client documentation: Codex MCP. Add the server to ~/.codex/config.toml, or to .codex/config.toml for a single project. Codex reads the token from an environment variable when it connects and sends it as Authorization: Bearer. ~/.codex/config.toml [mcp_servers.tape] url = "https://mcp.tapeapp.com/mcp" bearer_token_env_var = "TAPE_PAT" Export TAPE_PAT before you start Codex; if the variable is unset or empty, the server fails to start. Older Codex versions pick up stdio servers only: add experimental_use_rmcp_client = true under a [features] block above the server entry, or upgrade.

Client documentation: MCP connector. The Messages API calls the Tape MCP server directly through its MCP connector. Declare the server and reference it from a toolset: { "model": "claude-opus-5-5", "max_tokens": 4096, "mcp_servers": [ { "type": "url", "name": "tape", "url": "https://mcp.tapeapp.com/mcp", "authorization_token": "tape_pat_0a1b2c3d..." } ], "tools": [{ "type": "mcp_toolset", "mcp_server_name": "tape" }], "messages": [{ "role": "user", "content": "Which of my apps have records created this week?" }] } Send the beta header anthropic-beta: mcp-client-2025-11-20. Both halves are required: the API rejects mcp_servers without a matching mcp_toolset entry.

Configure a remote Streamable HTTP server with one custom header. Most clients accept a variation of: { "mcpServers": { "tape": { "url": "https://mcp.tapeapp.com/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer tape_pat_0a1b2c3d..." } } } } If the client speaks stdio only, use the mcp-remote bridge shown under Claude Desktop. There's no SSE endpoint to fall back to: Tape answers GET with 405. To test the endpoint by hand, point the MCP Inspector at https://mcp.tapeapp.com/mcp and add the Authorization header there.

Ask the assistant which Tape tools it has. A populated tool list shows that the client reaches the server. Ask it which Tape account it's connected as, for example "Which Tape user and organization are you connected as?" The assistant calls tape-fetch with type: "self", which needs no capability. The answer names your user and organization. Ask it which tools the token can use. The tool list from step 1 shows every tool, whatever the token's capabilities. The self answer's current_tool_access marks each tool available, partial or unavailable, with the missing_scopes to add. available means the capabilities don't block the tool; content access and roles still apply. Getting 401, or does the client ask you to sign in? See Troubleshooting a token connection.

Grant only what the assistant needs: You want the assistant to… Grant List apps, read views, and search apps:read Read records and their field values records:read List records shared with you records:read Create records apps:read + records:edit Update records records:read + records:edit (+ apps:read) Upload files records:edit Read comments and replies on records records.comments:read Post comments on records records.comments:edit Create apps (with their fields) and views apps:edit Change existing apps, or add fields to them apps:read + apps:edit Change an existing view apps:edit Look up other users in your organization organization:read Read the workspaces you belong to workspaces:read Create and rename workspaces workspaces:edit See automations, their setup and their run history, including credentials for connected systems automations:read Create, change, activate or pause automations automations:edit Trigger an automation manually automations:run Why does a write fail with only an edit capability? Editing doesn't include reading, and most write tools read before they write. Pair them, as the table does. Updating a record reads the app's schema only when you set a field that has no value yet. Without apps:read, a token updates many records and then fails on one. Search narrows its results instead of refusing: with only apps:read, it returns no records and no error. Grant both if the assistant should search across everything. Why do automations still fail with the right capability? tape-run-automation checks only automations:run. But automation IDs come only from tape-get-automations, and reading one uses tape-fetch. Both need automations:read, so pair them. Every automation route also requires the Admin role in the app's workspace, which no capability replaces. Without it, tape-get-automations and tape-get-runs return an empty page and no error ("none you administrate", not "none exist"). Everything else, including tape-fetch with type: "automation" or type: "automation_run", answers 404. A read-only assistant (apps:read and records:read only) can't read comments, see automations, list workspaces or look up colleagues: Tape refuses these calls instead of answering partially. Add records.comments:read, automations:read, workspaces:read and organization:read for whichever of these the assistant should reach. workspaces:edit reaches further than the MCP tools do No MCP tool deletes, but workspaces:edit covers deleting a workspace, and with it every app and record inside, in any other client or script that uses the token. Grant it only to a token that needs to create or rename workspaces. Creating a workspace also requires a token whose content access is All, and an organization role that permits creating workspaces.

automations:run reaches beyond the token An automation runs with the rights of the person who owns it. Triggering one can change and delete data in apps outside your token's content access, send email in someone else's name, call external systems, and run custom code. The tool's arguments don't show what the automation does. Grant it only when the assistant needs to trigger automations, and read the automation before you run it. A paused automation can still run this way: pausing stops only its trigger. automations:run neither implies nor requires automations:read or automations:edit.

The client can't connect, reports 401, or asks you to sign in to Tape even though you configured a token. The Authorization header doesn't reach the server, so Tape answers 401 and invites the client to sign in. Don't complete that sign-in if you meant to use a token: it connects without the token's limits. Check these points: The header name is exactly Authorization. The value starts with Bearer , including the space. If you used an environment variable, it's set in the environment the client was launched from. An unset variable leaves an empty Bearer value, which counts as no token. GUI apps often don't inherit a shell profile. no active user for the given API key, or a signature error. The token is wrong, revoked, or was altered on the way. Send it verbatim, with the tape_pat_ prefix in lower case. A tool returns 403 naming a missing capability. The token lacks a capability the tool needs, and capabilities are fixed at creation. Create a new token with the capability, switch the client over, and revoke the old one. See Choose capabilities. A tool returns 404 for a record, app or automation you know exists. Check the token's content access first: a resource outside it returns the same 404 as one that doesn't exist. For other causes, see Troubleshooting.

Select your profile picture, then select Preferences → Developer, and revoke the token there; see Revoke a token. Revoking takes effect on the next request and never affects your other tokens or your signed-in connections.

Personal access tokens how tokens work and how to limit them. Capabilities choose the right grants. Supported tools the capability each tool needs. Connect to Tape MCP connect by signing in instead. Security best practices what a token can reach, and how to bound it. Request limits the shared per-user budget.

With the server connected, an assistant can: Search across your apps and records, and follow references between them. Take stock of what reaches you outside the apps you can browse: the records shared with you individually, which no app-based listing returns. Read records, field values, apps, views, workspaces, and users, including the exact field structure of an app. Create and update records, post comments, and mint file upload tickets. Build structure: create and update workspaces, apps, fields, and views. Work with automations: read their definitions and run history, create and change them, and trigger one manually, which runs it with its owner's rights. Two things are absent by design, and neither is planned to change: No tool deletes anything. Not a record, comment, app, workspace, automation, field, or field option. Nothing grants people access. An assistant can't add or remove workspace members, or change who can see a record. A write can still lose data tape-update-database replaces a field's configuration as a whole. That's why it stays flagged destructive, even though it deletes nothing. Workspace reads are membership-scoped. They return the workspaces you belong to, not an inventory of your organization's workspaces. Your MCP client lists every tool, and what each one requires, when it connects. To see which ones your credential can use, check the connection.

The MCP server is a thin adapter in front of the public developer API. It holds no data and has no credential of its own. Every call that reads or changes your data uses your credential: the one your client received when you signed in, or the token you configured. MCP client ──HTTPS──▶ mcp.tapeapp.com ──▶ Tape Developer API ──▶ Tape (Claude Code, (tool calls) (api.tapeapp.com) Cursor, VS Code, …) The credential is yours, so the assistant reaches only what you can reach. Its capabilities narrow that further, and for a token, so does its content access. The automation capabilities are the exception. An automation runs with its owner's rights, not with your credential's. So automations:run can start one that reaches further than the credential, and automations:edit can rewrite what a live automation does before its own trigger fires it.

Besides tools, MCP defines resources: reference documents a client reads directly, without spending a tool call on them. Tape serves its reference specifications this way: how each field type expects a value to be shaped when you write it how to define a field how to write a record filter how a view is configured the grammar of an automation definition Resource URI Field values, the whole specification tape://docs/field-value-spec Field values, one field type tape://docs/field-value-spec/{field_type} App fields, the whole specification tape://docs/app-field-spec App fields, one field type tape://docs/app-field-spec/{field_type} Record filters, the whole specification tape://docs/filter-spec Record filters, one field type tape://docs/filter-spec/{field_type} Views, the whole specification tape://docs/view-spec Automations, the whole schema tape://docs/automation-schema Automations, one block type tape://docs/automation-schema/{block_type} All resources are JSON, and none needs a credential. They read no Tape data and return the same answer to every caller, so an assistant can read them before it connects. Every tool, by contrast, needs a credential: a sign-in or a token. Writing field values? The accepted shape of each value depends on the field's field_type, and several unrecognized shapes clear the field silently at 200. Read the specification before a write. The specification describes field types in general. For an app's own fields, their required flags and option lists, fetch the app itself. field_type is not type. A status field reads back as category, attachment and image both read back as file, and the single- and multi-value variants of one type accept different shapes. Your client can't read resources? Use tape-fetch. It serves all five specifications under type: "field_value_spec", "filter_spec", "view_spec", "app_field_spec" and "automation_schema". Unlike the resources, it needs a credential and takes no per-type narrowing, so "automation_schema" serves the whole ~75 KB catalog. Resource URIs are stable public API. Clients bookmark them, and a person who attached one to a conversation keeps a reference to that exact string. Tape treats a changed URI as a breaking change, the same as a renamed tool.

A client authenticates in one of two ways, and both act as you: Sign in with Tape Personal access token Setup Add the URL to your client and approve the connection in your browser Create a token in Tape and paste it into the client's configuration What it may do What your client asks for, usually every capability the Tape MCP tools use Only the capabilities you grant the token, for example read-only What it may reach Every workspace and app you can reach All, or only the workspaces and apps you select Works for Clients that support OAuth for remote MCP servers: Claude, Claude Code, ChatGPT, Cursor, VS Code, Codex, Gemini Enterprise and more Any client that can send a header, and servers or scripts without a browser Who can use it Organization members, admins and owners, not guests. Your organization may limit which clients members can connect Organization members, admins and owners, not guests Disconnect In Tape's settings, or by an organization admin Revoke the token Signing in is the default. It needs no secret in a config file, and the connection renews itself in the background. Under the hood it's the MCP authorization flow, OAuth 2.1 with PKCE, so any client that implements it works. See Build an MCP client. A token is the narrower choice. Use one when the assistant should only read, should reach only some of your data, or runs where nobody can sign in.

Any client that can call a remote MCP server over Streamable HTTP works: it signs in where it supports OAuth, or uses a token where it can set a request header. Clients that only run local servers connect through the mcp-remote bridge.

The endpoint answers POST only. It's stateless, mints no session ID, and answers GET and DELETE with 405. So opening the URL in a browser fails by design; to check the server, use the health endpoint. Request bodies are limited to 128 KB. The server rejects larger payloads before a tool runs. Rate limits are shared with the rest of your credentials. MCP tool calls draw on the same per-user budget as your other API traffic. Connecting a client doesn't buy extra throughput. See Request limits. Bytes never travel through MCP. tape-create-file-upload mints an upload ticket. The bytes go to the regular file endpoint. A failed tool call reaches the model. For a Tape API error, such as a record outside a token's content access or a capability a personal access token lacks, the server passes the API's own message through. The assistant can then explain or adapt. On a signed-in connection, a missing capability is not an error: your client asks you to approve the extra access, then retries the call.

Connect to Tape MCP: sign in from Claude, Claude Code, ChatGPT, Cursor, VS Code and other clients. Connect with a token: get read-only or narrower access, also for clients without a browser. Supported tools: look up what each tool does and which capability it needs. Security best practices: what a connection can reach, and how to bound it. Build an MCP client: what a client needs to connect to Tape. In the Help Center: Tape MCP

There is one official endpoint: https://mcp.tapeapp.com/mcp Anything else that claims to be Tape's MCP server is not. Connect only a client you trust with your data: it reaches everything its credential reaches. It may send what it reads to the model provider it runs on, or to other systems it's connected to. When you sign in, the consent screen names the client that is asking. A client Tape hasn't verified is marked Unverified. Its name is self-asserted, so approve only a connection you started yourself. Organization owners and admins can go further and allow Approved MCP clients only. See For organization admins. The server itself holds no credential that can read or change your data. Every call that touches your data uses the credential your client sent, for that one request only: the access token from signing in, or a personal access token, never your browser session. The credential is the boundary, so choosing and scoping it is the main control you have.

Signing in is broad by design. A signed-in connection reaches every workspace and app you can reach. Clients ask for every capability the Tape MCP tools use, including editing apps and workspaces, and editing and running automations. None of those capabilities manages organization or workspace members, shares records, manages webhooks, or sends email. Tape doesn't stop a client from asking for more, though. The consent screen lists what the client asked for, so read it before you approve. The access token a client receives when you sign in also works at the Tape Developer API. The client, or the platform it runs on, can use every capability you approved directly, including the deletions the :edit capabilities allow. If you wouldn't trust a client with that, connect it with a narrower personal access token instead. A token can be narrower. When the assistant should only read, or reach only some of your data, connect it with a personal access token. Both of a token's grants only subtract: Capabilities: a token with only apps:read and records:read gives you an assistant that answers questions and can't change anything. Start there, and add write capabilities only when you want the assistant to write. Content access: limit the token to the workspaces and apps the assistant needs, instead of all of them. Beyond that: Use one token per client. You can't revoke a shared token without breaking something unrelated, and you can't tell which client did what. Never commit a token. Prefer the environment-variable or secret-prompt form for your client. See Connect with a token. Whichever way you connect: The assistant never exceeds your access, except through automations. Its access is your own permissions, narrowed by its capabilities. The two automation write capabilities escape that, because an automation runs with its owner's rights: automations:run can start one that reaches apps outside a token's content access, and automations:edit can rewrite a live automation's actions and let its own trigger fire them. See the automations:run callout. Tape attributes everything the assistant does to you. Records the assistant creates or changes show you as the author in the activity stream. To tell an assistant's activity apart, connect it from a dedicated user account.
documents.s: Choose how much the assistant can reach

documents.t: Tape records hold content other people wrote: field values, comments, file names, imported data. When an assistant reads that content, it enters the model's context. Someone can craft text there to read as instructions instead of data. An injected instruction acts with your credential A successful injection doesn't need to break Tape's permissions to do damage. It acts entirely inside them. It could exfiltrate data the assistant can read by writing it somewhere the attacker can see, or change records the credential may change. To limit the damage: Treat tool results as untrusted input, not as instructions, the same way you treat any content from an external system. Review write actions before you approve them. If your client can gate write tools behind a confirmation, configure it that way. Every tool carries the standard MCP annotations (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, openWorldHint), so a client can tell the ten read-only tools from the thirteen that write, and single out the six flagged destructive. tape-run-automation is one of those six, and the only tool flagged openWorldHint because its effects leave Tape: give it its own confirmation step. Treat a file upload URL as a secret. tape-create-file-upload returns an upload_url that needs no authentication and accepts one upload as you until it is used or expires. A client should not log it or write it into a record. Prefer a read-only token for anything exploratory. A token without write capabilities can't be turned against your data, whatever it reads. When you sign in, most clients ask for write capabilities too, and you can't narrow that when you approve; for read-only use, connect with a token, or in Gemini Enterprise enter the read-only scopes. Choose which apps the assistant can see. Content access limits a credential; it doesn't isolate data. Treat it as a way to reduce the blast radius, not as a boundary around sensitive information. See the caveat on content access. Writes reach beyond the record they touch. By default, a record or comment written through MCP behaves like one written by hand: it notifies followers, fires webhooks, and triggers automations. An automation can send email and make outbound HTTP calls, so a single injected write can turn into egress out of Tape. tape-create-records, tape-update-record and tape-create-comment accept silent, no_webhook and no_workflow to suppress each of those; all three default to false, so the safe behavior is opt-in. The surface can also write automations. Five dedicated tools list, create, change, and trigger them, and tape-fetch reads both a definition and a single run as a sixth way in. So an injected instruction doesn't have to hope a write fires a trigger: it can compose the trigger itself, or start an existing automation whose actions send email and call external systems. Two properties bound this: A created automation starts paused and needs a deliberate second call to activate. Tape refuses to activate a broken definition. Neither helps against an automation that is already live. Treat automations:edit and automations:run as write capabilities of a heavier class than records:edit.

Some limits are structural. They hold whatever the credential allows: Nothing on this surface deletes. There is no tool to delete a record, comment, app, workspace, automation, field, or field option. Removing them is a human action in the Tape app. For fields, see Change an app. Nothing grants people access. An assistant can't add or remove workspace members, or change who can see a record. No arbitrary HTTP, and no file downloads. There is no proxy tool an injected instruction could point at a URL of its choosing. These limits are deliberate and aren't planned to change. The limits bound the tools, not the credential Most :edit capabilities go beyond these limits through any other client or script that uses the credential: records:edit permits deleting records. apps:edit permits deleting apps, fields, and views. records.comments:edit permits deleting your own comments. automations:edit permits deleting automations. workspaces:edit permits deleting a workspace and everything inside it. So "the assistant can't delete anything" is true of the tool list and false of the credential. Grant accordingly.

Disconnecting is the kill switch, and it's cheap. It takes effect on the next request. Nothing is cached, and nothing needs re-issuing. A signed-in client: disconnect it in Tape. See Manage your connections. Organization admins can disconnect a client for one member or for everyone. A token: select your profile picture, then select Preferences → Developer, and revoke the token there. Removing a client in Tape's settings ends every connection you have to that client. claude.ai, Claude Desktop, and Claude Code, for example, are all the one client Claude. Removing a client or revoking a token never affects your other clients, tokens or account. If a token may have leaked, revoke it first and investigate afterwards. Secret scanners recognize the tape_pat_ prefix, so they can spot a leaked token automatically. Disconnect a client when you stop using it. Don't leave a live connection, or a token in a config file you've forgotten about.

Connect to Tape MCP sign in from your client and manage your connections. Connect with a token set up a read-only or narrower connection. Capabilities choose the fewest grants that work. Personal access tokens how content access works. Supported tools check which tools write, and which are flagged destructive.

Tool Purpose Capability Finding your way around tape-get-apps Every app the token can see, with its workspace apps:read tape-list-shared-records Records the token reaches individually, outside the apps it is granted records:read tape-search Full-text search across apps and records apps:read or records:read tape-fetch One app, record, view, workspace, automation or automation run by id varies by type tape-get-workspaces The workspaces you belong to workspaces:read tape-get-users Find people in your organization by name organization:read Records tape-query-records List an app's records, or run a saved view records:read (+ apps:read) tape-create-records Create one or more records apps:read + records:edit tape-update-record Change field values on one record records:read + records:edit (+ apps:read) tape-create-file-upload Mint an upload ticket for an attachment records:edit Comments tape-get-comments A record's comments and their replies records.comments:read tape-create-comment Post a comment, optionally with @mentions records.comments:edit Structure tape-create-database Create an app, optionally with its fields apps:edit tape-update-database Change an app and its fields apps:read + apps:edit tape-create-view Create a saved view apps:edit tape-update-view Change a saved view apps:edit tape-create-workspace Create a workspace workspaces:edit tape-update-workspace Change a workspace's name, description or icon workspaces:edit Automations tape-get-automations Automations you administrate automations:read tape-get-runs Executions: what ran, when, and whether it worked automations:read tape-create-automation Create an automation, paused automations:edit tape-update-automation Change, activate or pause an automation automations:edit tape-run-automation Run one automation immediately automations:run A capability in parentheses is conditional: only some calls need it. Without apps:read, tape-update-record fails on those calls, while tape-query-records still answers in full and only its diagnostics degrade. Grant apps:read alongside either way; the capability table shows the same information by task. Can a tool delete anything or grant access? No. No tool removes a record, comment, app, workspace, automation, field, or field option; a person removes them in the Tape app. No tool adds or removes members, or changes who can see a record. tape-update-database is still flagged destructive, for the reason in its section.

tape-get-apps Returns every app the token can see, with the workspace each one belongs to. Start here when you have no IDs yet: Tape organizes data as workspaces, which hold apps, which hold records. The result isn't paginated, so you get the complete picture in one response. Example prompts: "What apps do we have in Tape?" "Which apps are in the Sales workspace?" "Find the app where we track candidates" Good to know: "Every app the token can see" is not "everything the token can reach". Someone can share a record with you individually inside an app you can't open, and this tool lists no app for it. tape-list-shared-records is the other half of the picture. Only database apps have records. An app has the type database, dashboard or form, and only database apps have records and fields. Filter on type before you pass an app_id to a tool that reads records. Two apps in different workspaces can share a name.

tape-list-shared-records Lists the records the token reaches individually, through a grant on the record itself or a matching permission rule, without app-level access to the database app they live in. It's the only tool that lists these records: tape-query-records needs an app ID, so no app-based listing reliably reaches past the app boundary. Rows are previews (IDs, app name, title, link, author, and creation time, no field values), newest first, with up to 100 records per page. Example prompts: "What is shared with me?" "Take stock of everything this account can reach" "Are there records I can see outside my own apps?" "List what is shared with me and summarize the newest one" Good to know: Pair it with tape-get-apps. That one lists what the assistant can browse; this one lists what reaches it from outside. Without it, an assistant asked what it can see lists everything it can browse and reports that as the complete answer. "Shared with you" isn't exact, in both directions. A permission rule can place a record here because you created it or because a field names you, with no share involved. So these are records you can reach, not necessarily records someone shared with you. And a record shared with you inside an app you can access, through workspace membership or a grant on the app itself, is absent on purpose. Read that one with tape-query-records on its app. The app_id on a row is usually an app the token can't read. So tape-fetch with type: "app" on it, or tape-query-records with that ID, is often refused. That's expected, not a fault. To read a row in full, use tape-fetch with type: "record", which checks permission on the record itself. There is no total, and an empty list doesn't prove an account reaches nothing. For a token limited to selected workspaces or apps, Tape narrows this listing to them as well, without saying so. Tape doesn't record or return the date a record was shared with you.

tape-search Searches across every app and record the token can reach, best match first, including records shared with it individually in apps it can't otherwise open. Use it when you have words, not IDs: a record someone described in prose, or an app with an approximate name. Results are previews (IDs, names, titles, a link, and creation times), enough to identify something and then read it, with up to 100 results per page. Example prompts: "Find the record for the Meyer project" "Is there already a record for this customer?" "Which apps mention onboarding?" "Show me everything created in the CRM workspace last week" Good to know: Search returns no field values and no total count. Use has_more to decide whether more results exist. Search can't express "all records where status is open". That's tape-query-records with filters. Search can confirm that a record exists, but can't answer "what do I have access to". It needs matching words. For that question, use tape-list-shared-records. A token with only apps:read searches successfully and returns no records at all, because search narrows instead of refusing.

tape-fetch Reads one app, record, saved view, workspace, automation, or automation run by its ID. With type: "self", it returns the user and organization the token acts as, which is the fastest way to confirm a connection. Its current_tool_access shows which tools the connection can use. It also serves the five static specifications that are otherwise MCP resources: field_value_spec, filter_spec, view_spec, app_field_spec and automation_schema. Example prompts: "Which Tape account am I connected as?" "Show me the field structure of the Deals app" "What does this view filter on?" "Read record 4711" Good to know: Each arm needs a different capability, so one token reads some and not others. The automation and automation_run arms need automations:read, which a normal read-only token doesn't carry. Reading a run also needs the Admin role in the app's workspace. self and the five documents need no capability at all. One arm isn't addressed by id. type: "automation_run" takes run_id instead: a string that only tape-get-runs produces. Pass it back exactly as you received it; don't parse it into a number. See Read one run. No documentation arm takes a per-type narrowing, so each serves its whole document. That matters most for automation_schema, which is around 75 KB. The resource form narrows to one block type (tape://docs/automation-schema/{block_type}). Prefer it if your client reads resources; the arm exists for clients that can't. A Tape ID is unique only within its own kind, and the sequences overlap. A wrong type doesn't reliably fail: reading a record ID with type: "app" can return a real, unrelated app. Take type from wherever you got the ID.

tape-get-workspaces Returns the workspaces the token can reach, each with its visibility type: open, default, closed or private. Read the type before you create anything inside a workspace, because it decides who else sees what you put there. Example prompts: "Which workspaces do I have access to?" "Is the Finance workspace private?" "Where should I put a new app for the recruiting team?" Good to know: This returns the workspaces the account is a member of, not an inventory of the organization. Other workspaces may exist that this token can't see.

tape-get-users Looks up people in the organization by name and returns their user_id, which an @mention needs. To assign someone in a user field, you often don't need it: Tape resolves an unambiguous plain name on write. Look up the ID when a wrong guess would matter. Example prompts: "What is Will's user id?" "Are there two people called Müller in our organization?" "Who should I assign this to, find me Juliet" Good to know: Returns only IDs and names, never email addresses or phone numbers. Can't list the whole organization. A query is required. Excludes deactivated users, so you won't find someone who has left. To find out who you are, use tape-fetch with type: "self" instead.

tape-query-records Lists the records of one database app, or runs one of its saved views. Each record comes back with its field values, so you rarely need a follow-up read per row. Supports filters by field value, selecting only the fields you need, and pages of up to 500 records. Example prompts: "List all open deals over 10,000 euro" "Run the 'Overdue tasks' view and summarize it" "Which records in this database have no owner set?" "Export the contacts database as a table" Good to know: Read the filter specification (tape://docs/filter-spec) before you write filters. The accepted shape depends on the field's field_type, and field_type is not type: a status field reads back as category, attachment and image both as file. A field with no value is left out of the response, not returned empty. So a misspelled entry in select_fields looks exactly like an empty field. Check unresolved_fields, which lists every selection that matched nothing. apps:read is conditional here and, unlike on tape-update-record, never makes the call fail. The tool uses it only to explain an entry in unresolved_fields. Without it, the records still come back in full, and that entry's reason degrades to unknown. Filters don't touch the app schema at all.

tape-create-records Creates one or more records in a database app, up to 10 per call. Tape creates the records published, and everyone who can see the database sees them right away. There is no draft state on this surface. Example prompts: "Add a record for the call I had with Meyer GmbH today" "Create three tasks from these bullet points" "Log this invoice in the accounting database" Good to know: Not idempotent, and there is no undo. No tool on this surface removes a record. Calling it twice creates two sets of records. After a failure or timeout, check with tape-search or tape-query-records before you retry. By default, a created record notifies followers, fires webhooks, and triggers automations, like one created by hand. silent, no_webhook and no_workflow suppress each of those, and all three default to false. The same three flags exist on tape-update-record and tape-create-comment, and nowhere else on this surface. Tape validates field keys before it creates anything. The tool refuses an unknown key, a read-only field, or a whole field object copied from a read, because Tape would accept all three without error and write nothing. A refusal means no records were created, not some of them.

tape-update-record Changes field values on one existing record. This is a partial update: fields you name change, fields you don't name keep their value, and null clears a field. Example prompts: "Set this deal to Won" "Add Juliet as a second assignee on this task" "Clear the due date on record 4711" "Correct the spelling of the company name" Good to know: Any field that holds a list of entries is replaced as a whole. What you send becomes the entire value, and everything you leave out is deleted, without notice, at HTTP 200. This covers users, categories, phone, email, link, relations, attachments, images, and checklists. "Add Juliet as an assignee" means reading the record first and sending the existing assignees back plus Juliet. There is no undo. Updating a record reads the app's schema only when you set a field that has no value yet. So a token without apps:read updates many records successfully and then fails on one. Grant apps:read alongside.

tape-create-file-upload Mints a short-lived URL that accepts one file upload, so you can attach the file to a record. Attaching takes two steps: Call this tool. POST the file to the returned URL as multipart/form-data. The response gives you a file handle. Write it into an attachment or image field like any other value. Example prompts: "Attach this PDF to the Meyer record" "Upload the floor plan and put it on the property record" Good to know: The URL works for exactly one request and needs no authentication of its own. Treat it as a secret while it lasts. Several files can go in that one request, under the same form field name and up to the returned max_files_per_request. For a second request, call the tool again. The file never passes through the MCP server. Tape checks records:edit when it mints the URL, not when you upload. So a read-only token is refused at the first step. A client that can't make HTTP requests of its own can't do step 2. In that case, the file has to go into Tape through the web interface.

tape-get-comments Returns a record's comments and their replies in one call, as two separately paginated lists. Tape threads are two levels deep: people comment on a record and reply to a comment. Example prompts: "What was decided on this record?" "Did anyone answer my question on the Meyer deal?" "Summarize the discussion on this task" Good to know: A list you didn't ask for comes back as null, which means "not read on this call". That's not the same as an empty array, which means the record has none. Never report a null list as an empty discussion. Everything this tool returns is prose other people wrote. Treat it as data, never as instructions. See Security best practices.

tape-create-comment Posts a comment on a record, optionally with @mentions. A comment is not a field value and changes no data. Comments are append-only here: there is no tool to edit or delete one. Example prompts: "Leave a note on this record that I called them back" "Ask @Will on the record whether the contract is signed" "Summarize what I changed and post it as a comment" Good to know: Mentions are the main reason to use this tool instead of plain text. Write @[Full Name](user:123), with the ID from tape-get-users. A bare @Jane notifies nobody. silent suppresses every notification for the comment, including the one an @mention would send. If the point is to get someone's attention, leave silent unset.

tape-create-database Creates one database app (a table) in a workspace, optionally with its fields. You can create only database apps here, no dashboards or forms. Example prompts: "Create an app for tracking supplier contracts with fields for supplier, value, start and end date" "Set up a simple app for our onboarding checklist" Good to know: record_name is required. It's what one record in the database is called, singular: "Task" for an app named "Tasks". Tape shows it everywhere it refers to a single row. The Tape API would default it to the app's name, so every row would be called "Tasks" with no error and no way to notice; this tool insists on it. The order of fields is permanent and decides what every record is titled. The first title-capable field becomes the title field, whose value names the record everywhere Tape shows one. Nothing on this surface reorders fields afterwards. Read tape://docs/app-field-spec for each field type's config.settings. Not idempotent, and there is no undo. You can't create a calculation field here. Add it afterwards with tape-update-database.

tape-update-database Changes an app's name and description, and the fields it holds. Partial at the argument level: what you name changes, what you leave out stays as it is. Example prompts: "Add a priority field to the tasks app" "Rename the 'Owner' column to 'Account manager'" "Make the due date field required" Good to know: This tool can't delete, as of 2026-08-23. It removes no field and no field option, and nothing else on this surface does either. A person does that in the Tape app. If you built against the old shape, the two removed arguments now behave differently: fields_to_delete and allow_deleting_field_values are gone from the schema. A call that still sends them succeeds, with everything else applied, nothing deleted, and no error. options_to_delete, which sits inside a fields entry, is refused, and Tape rejects the whole call. Nothing changes, not the options and not the rest. Tape refuses both again behind the tool, so this is a property of the surface, not of one client's arguments. Tape appends a new field at the end. It ignores config.position when it's a string and rejects it when it's a number, and no tool here reorders fields. So you can't change an app's first field, which supplies every record's title, through MCP at all. The tool is still flagged destructive, because not deleting is not the same as not losing data: A field entry is a replace, not a patch. config.label is required on every entry, and every top-level config key you leave out is reset. One exception: what you leave out inside config.settings survives. A label-only change keeps a number field's unit and decimals and a category field's options. Do not echo settings back to protect it. An options entry with an existing id renames that option everywhere, so every record that holds it reads differently afterwards. The whole call is all or nothing.

tape-create-view Creates a saved view on an app: a stored query with its own filters, sort, grouping, and layout. A view is the visible way to save a query for people. To filter records without storing anything, use tape-query-records. Example prompts: "Create a board view grouped by status in the deals app" "Add a view showing only tasks due this week, sorted by priority" "Make a view of contacts without an email address" Good to know: Some arguments succeed without doing what you asked. A sort_by that names a field that exists nowhere is dropped without notice, and Tape creates the view unsorted. sort_desc without sort_by is discarded. Read the returned view instead of assuming. No tool on this surface makes a view the default or makes it private. There is no argument for either, so asking for one has no effect. A view created here is public. Everyone who can see the app sees it.

tape-update-view Changes a saved view's name, layout, filters, sort, grouping, or display settings. Example prompts: "Rename this view to 'Sprint board'" "Filter this view to open items only" "Group the view by owner instead of by status" Good to know: An argument you leave out stays as it is, but an argument you send replaces what's stored. filters, fields, split_by, table and board are replaced as whole collections and never merged: send one filter and the view has one filter. Read the view first with tape-fetch and type: "view". The same silent outcomes as on tape-create-view apply. name: null keeps the current name instead of clearing it. table and board read back null for the layout the view isn't in. That's a reporting artifact: those settings come back unchanged when you switch back.

tape-create-workspace Creates a workspace, the top-level container that holds apps. type is required and accepts private, open or closed. The tool doesn't offer default on purpose: making a workspace the organization's default is a decision for a person in Tape. Example prompts: "Create a private workspace called Recruiting 2026" Good to know: Requires a token whose content access is All, plus an organization role that permits creating workspaces. Tape refuses a token limited to selected workspaces and apps outright. The refusal names no capability, so a broader set of capabilities won't fix it. See Content access. Not idempotent, and nothing on this surface deletes a workspace. Ask which type is wanted before you create one; private is the only one that can't over-share.

tape-update-workspace Changes a workspace's name, description, or icon. Nothing else about a workspace can change here. The route also requires the Admin role in the workspace, which no capability expresses. Example prompts: "Rename the Sales workspace to Revenue" "Give the Recruiting workspace a proper description" Good to know: You can't change the workspace type on this surface. The type decides who reaches what's inside. Tape ignores an attempt without notice and answers success with the old type. You can't add or remove members either. Both are decisions for a person in Tape. Neither null nor an empty string is accepted, so you can't clear a description or icon here. This differs from tape-update-record, where null clears a field.

An automation is a saved program that belongs to one app: a trigger, an optional filter, and an ordered list of actions. These tools need their own three capabilities, which a normal read-only token doesn't carry and which a token can hold independently of one another. See the capability table. Every automation route also requires the Admin role in the app's workspace. That's a role, not a capability, so no broader token fixes it, and no automation tool reports it as a capability problem: tape-get-automations and tape-get-runs return an empty page and no error. An account that administrates nothing sees exactly what an organization with no automations sees. Everything else, including tape-fetch with type: "automation" or type: "automation_run", answers 404, the same answer as for an automation that doesn't exist.
