tape-get-automations Lists the automations the account administrates, one page at a time. It's the usual way to get an automation ID; tape-get-runs also carries automation_id on every row it returns. Example prompts: "What automations run on the deals app?" "Is there an automation that sends the welcome email?" "Which automations are paused?" Good to know: An empty list doesn't prove the organization has no automations. Automations live in apps, and this tool shows only those in workspaces where the account is an admin. Say "I can't see any", not "there are none". trigger, filter and actions come back in Tape's own automation grammar. Read tape://docs/automation-schema for what the shapes mean. Send them back to tape-update-automation unchanged unless you mean to change them.

tape-get-runs Lists executions of automations: what ran, when, and whether it worked. Every filter is optional. Example prompts: "Did the invoice automation run last night?" "Show me everything that failed today" "How often did this automation run this week?" Good to know: Tape keeps only about 30 days of runs. An automation with no runs may not have run this month, which is no evidence that it never runs. Simulation runs in the Tape interface never appear here. type is manual for a run that somebody or tape-run-automation started by hand, and regular for one a trigger fired.

tape-fetch with type: "automation_run" Reads one execution, including the log of every step: the trigger, the filter, and one entry per action, with one entry per iteration for actions inside a loop. Use this arm for "why did that fail". Example prompts: "Why did this automation run fail?" "What exactly did the automation do on this record?" Good to know: It's addressed by run_id, never by id. A run_id is a string and comes only from a tape-get-runs row. Pass it back exactly as you received it. Sending an automation_id instead doesn't reliably fail: runs and automations use separate sequences, so the same number is often valid for both, and an unrelated run's log can come back with no error at all. To diagnose a failure, find the log entry whose status is failure and read its messages. That names the step that broke, which the run's own error_message usually doesn't. The action_id on a log entry points at a node in the automation's stored actions list. Tape re-mints those IDs whenever tape-update-automation replaces that list. An action_id from an older run may no longer match anything in the current definition. Check the entry's label as well before you tell somebody which action failed. A refusal tells you nothing about the run. Tape refuses a run that never existed, one past the retention window, one deleted, one that belongs to somebody else, and one in a workspace you don't administrate in the same way, so nobody can probe run IDs.

tape-create-automation Creates an automation in an app. Tape creates it paused, and it doesn't run until somebody activates it with tape-update-automation. Example prompts: "Create an automation that sets the status to Overdue when the due date passes" "Draft an automation that posts a comment whenever a deal is won" Good to know: Read tape://docs/automation-schema before you compose trigger, filter or actions. broken is false in every response and is no verdict on what you wrote. Tape checks validity when you activate, and refuses activation if the definition is invalid. That refusal is the real check. Nothing on this surface deletes an automation. A wrong create leaves a paused automation for a person to remove in Tape, so prefer correcting one over creating a second.

tape-update-automation Changes an automation's name, description, trigger, filter, or actions, and activates or pauses it. Send only what you mean to change. Example prompts: "Pause the invoice reminder automation" "Activate the automation I created earlier" "Change this automation to fire on Won instead of Qualified" Good to know: Activating is a real-world event. is_paused: false makes the automation run against live data from that moment. It sends email, calls external systems, and changes or deletes records according to its actions. Show a person what it does before you activate it. null clears description, trigger and filter, unlike on some other update tools, but not name, which rejects it. null on a filter is the dangerous one: an automation with no filter acts on every trigger event, which is wider than before, not narrower. actions replaces and doesn't merge, and sending [] leaves the automation broken.
documents.s: Change, activate or pause an automation

documents.t: tape-run-automation Runs one automation immediately, with real effects. It's the only tool whose effects leave Tape, and it's annotated openWorldHint: true for exactly that reason. Example prompts: "Run the monthly report automation now" "Trigger the welcome sequence for this new contact" Good to know: This runs a program somebody else wrote, and its effects aren't limited to Tape. Its actions can send email to real people, call external systems, and create, change, or delete records. None of that is visible from this tool's arguments. Read the automation first with tape-fetch and type: "automation", and say what it does. There is no undo. Success means "accepted", never "it ran". The response has no run ID, on purpose, and the automation's own filter still applies. A record that doesn't match produces no run at all, and this call still succeeds. Poll tape-get-runs for what happened. You can still run a paused automation this way. Pausing stops its trigger; it doesn't disable manual runs.

MCP tool calls draw on the same per-user budget as the rest of the Tape API: 2,000 credits per minute. Everything that acts as you shares it: signed-in MCP clients and other connected apps, your personal access tokens, and your user API key. So connecting another client doesn't buy extra throughput; see Request limits. The base request cost is 10 credits, which would be 200 calls per minute. Several routes charge a multiple of it, so treat 200 as a ceiling, not an expectation: A search costs 50 credits (5× base), and so does each further page of results. That works out to roughly 40 searches per minute. Reading one view with tape-fetch costs 20. A single tool call can bill more than one route: tape-fetch with type: "app" or type: "workspace" makes two. Where an endpoint charges above base, its API resource page says so. Every response carries X-Retry-Remaining and X-Retry-Reset. A refused call still costs credits, because capability checks run after rate limiting. Retrying a call your token can't make uses up the budget without ever succeeding. Rate limited? Ask the assistant to work in smaller batches and to stop searching in parallel. Prefer one tape-query-records call with a filter over many tape-fetch calls in a loop. When you need the complete picture, prefer tape-get-apps (with tape-list-shared-records) over repeated searches.
